CORRECTION TO THE COMMENT ABOVE: THE RUN WAS NEVER PARKED, AND THIS COORDINATOR ASSERTED REALISED HARM THAT DID NOT OCCUR. That comment said the run is unresumable and would be skipped on every sweep forever. Four minutes later it transitioned waiting → dispatched, overwrote its own declaration, and is running normally. Its manifest has since read blocked and it is still generating.

What was wrong: the wait declaration was a mid-turn checkpoint, not a verdict. The worker wrote it while working, exactly as the contract instructs — write your manifest with what you know now — and replaced it as its own understanding changed. Reading a manifest field as a terminal state is the error this plan documents repeatedly, and it was committed here by the coordinator that documented it, against its own fleet, within an hour of recording the rule a third time.

What survives, and it is the part worth keeping. The trap is real and remains unclosed: a wait whose wait_terminal carries only exit: forms while its probe prints output can never match, because terminal values are matched against the probe's last line and the exit: forms stand in only for a silent probe. A worker that ends its turn holding such a declaration is parked with no sweep that can wake it. This run escaped by continuing past its own checkpoint; a worker out of turns would not have. So the exposure is latent rather than realised, which is a materially smaller claim than the one made above and the honest size of it.

The distinction is exactly the one this plan exists to draw. A latent trap and a realised failure justify different urgency, and collapsing them inflates a finding in the direction that feels responsible — which is how an over-stated defect earns a fix it did not need while a real one waits. The template repair still wants the two one-line additions named above; it does not want them as an emergency.

And the operational decision was right for the stated reason rather than by luck. The run was left alive because its process was generating, on the rule that a coordinator must not kill a worker on the strength of a manifest field. It then proved the rule by recovering itself. Had it been stopped when its manifest first read waiting, the work would have been destroyed and the finding would have looked confirmed.

Two defects in the manifest template produce the malformed wait declarations the classifier then refuses. Both are in prompts.py, and together they outrank the classifier repair: that one stops a correct run being mislabelled, these stop the malformed input existing.

A placeholder that names a type teaches nothing. Line 236 reads wait_probe: <only when setting status to waiting: the shell-free argument vector that answers the condition, run in your worktree>. "Shell-free argument vector" is a description of a type, in prose, inside a placeholder. The second is a missing state, not a wording defect, and it is the one that explains "no wait". Line 221 tells a worker running out of turns mid-wait to set status: waiting and fill the four wait keys — correct, and the only checkpoint idiom the template offers. Nothing covers a worker that is resumed and not waiting. So a worker resumed after the serve restart reached for the only shape available and wrote wait_condition: no wait — process was killed mid-turn by a deliberate server restart. It was not misreading the template; it was using the one slot it had. A resume checkpoint is a different state from a wait and the block has no room for it.

That reframes the classifier finding: the declaration is genuinely self-contradictory and the classifier is right to reject it, but the worker was correct to write something and had nowhere correct to write it. Fixing only the classifier leaves every resumed worker producing the same shape.

blockers is a field a promotion reads, so this is not cosmetic: a worker writing "no blockers were found" as a bullet inside its evidence prose now registers a top-level blockers value it never declared. The continuation form is the manifest's own idiom — every list field in a well-formed manifest is written as - item lines beneath its key.

One direction loses a field the worker wrote; the other invents one it did not.

A second review finding, recorded as provenance: the decorated matcher is not symmetric with the scalar reader for a JSON-literal value — baseline_suite: {…} parses whole when plain, while the mechanism comment claims decorated lines are recognised only within the manifest vocabulary, a claim asserted for prose bullets and not for an indented vocabulary-word bullet under a prior field.

The node delivered what it was asked and the regression is a side effect its own gate could not see, because the gate asserted the new decorated forms rather than the unchanged behaviour of the old ones. The measure that would have caught it is a corpus check: every manifest already on disk parses identically before and after.

It was tested instead. Four synthetic shapes that force a mapping or a sequence into key position — a flow mapping as a top-level key, an explicit-key mapping, a flow sequence as a key, and a mapping key nested under a field — all parse cleanly, so the instrument was aimed at the real population rather than trusted on synthetics: 3,704 real manifests on this host, 2,963 parsed, 741 declared ManifestParseError refusals, and zero escaped exceptions of any type. The 741 are the positive control, since an unaimed scan and a genuine absence return the same empty result. The merged repair stands.

The general rule this establishes, which is worth more than the claim was: a dead review's last sentence is a hypothesis, not a finding. The signature of this failure is a process ending mid-investigation, so its final text is by construction the thing it was about to check rather than the thing it concluded. Reading it as a result inverts the reliability of the most suspect sentence in the stream. Recover the claim, then range an instrument over the real population before recording it either way.

A second lesson, from getting it wrong. The first of these two was promoted before checking whether it could be resumed, and it could: its live pointer carried a captured session, and promotion deletes the pointer crew resume depends on. The second had session_id: null, so no resume path existed and promoting it was correct. The discriminator is the live pointer's own session_id, and it is not visible in the classification — both rows render identically as a dead review. Read that field before reconciling any run, because the two cases look the same and only one is recoverable.

So the write-early mitigation works, and that is the problem. It was adopted because seven reviews had done substantial work and produced no record; it did exactly what it was asked to do. What it produced here is a record scoring every dimension at precisely 12 with findings: [] — an initialisation that a gate keyed on existence-and-parse accepts as an independent review. The failure mode was not removed; it was converted.

The conversion is a loss, not a wash, and the reason is asymmetric. A dead review that wrote nothing is honest: the run sits in scoring, promotion is refused, and a coordinator sees exactly what happened. A dead review that wrote a skeleton is not: the run advances to promotable and the next reader sees a verdict. Absence announces itself; a placeholder does not. Measured across both projects today, the two states are indistinguishable at every surface a coordinator or a classifier reads.

This is the same shape this plan exists for. A true statement — the review record exists and parses — standing in for the one that was needed, which is that a reviewer considered the work. The census figure to carry forward is eight deaths, of which one left a skeleton; expect that ratio to invert as the instruction propagates, because the instruction is working.

Recorded as a failed run with classification infrastructure-failure rather than discarded, so the death stays countable and the skeleton stays inspectable. Its parent run is not promoted on that record; a re-review is queued.

Every pointer that leaves is reported as promoted, so the display cannot tell work banked from work erased. reckon/crew/recovery.py:2838:

changes.append((departed, str(known[run_id]["state"]), "promoted"))

Measured rather than reasoned. A peer coordinator discarded the pointer from a failed dispatch with crew discard — whose own help text says it removes a pointer without recording promoted evidence. The ticker emitted abandoned → promoted and the unpromoted counter fell by one. Verified here against the committed ledger: 0 rows for that run id, against 1,072 total. Nothing was promoted, no evidence exists, and the display said the work was banked.

promoted there means the pointer disappeared, which is the one inference a departure cannot support. A pointer departs on promotion, on discard, and on any rollback that manages to unlink it — work banked, work erased, and work lost. The ticker renders all three identically, and the counter falls the same amount for each.

The direction of the error is what makes it serious. An orchestrator clearing a backlog by discarding watches its inbox drain while the ledger stays still, and is congratulated at every step. That is the same reward shape as a review scoring higher for finding nothing: the display pays out for the action that destroys the evidence.

The repair is the rule this sprint keeps arriving at, on a fourth surface. Do not infer the verdict from the free-running observation; require the declared record. A departure resolves to promoted only when a ledger row for that run id exists, and otherwise to a state with its own word — discarded where the pointer was removed deliberately, something else again where it simply vanished. Two declared integers rather than a substring search; findings counted rather than prose; a ledger row present rather than a pointer absent. Same move each time.

The file is held by a-scoring-run-dispatches-its-own-review and this is adjacent to that node rather than inside it, so it is sequenced behind it rather than folded in.

--time-budget is not a ceiling. It is exceeded in the majority of runs, and nothing enforces it. Flagged by a peer coordinator from a single 58% overrun; measured here across the committed ledger.

MeasureCount
ledger rows carrying both a stated budget and a measured duration398
overran on wall time219 (55%)
overran on worker time, so not wall-clock idling217 (55%)
overran on a first attempt, so no resume accumulation168
worst first-attempt overrun7.38× — 11,063s against 1,500s

The resume caveat was checked and does not rescue it. Sixty-one of the 398 rows are resumed runs whose wall time legitimately accumulates across attempts, and the worst raw figure — 20.9×, 62,714 seconds against 3,000 — is one of those. Excluding every resumed run still leaves 168 first-attempt overruns, and the worker-time count matches the wall-time count almost exactly (217 against 219), so the overruns are work rather than waiting.

What this invalidates is not the budget but everything written on top of it. The orchestration rules about bounded slices, the recovery reasoning that treats a long-running node as anomalous, and every brief either coordinator has written carrying a --time-budget value all assume a bound the surface does not provide. A worker that finishes inside its budget is keeping a convention; it is not being held to anything. A coordinator reading an overrun as a signal of trouble is reading the ordinary case — it happens more often than not.

It also changes what an overrun means as evidence. The review that died at 66 turns ran 58% past its budget, and the first objection raised against reading its terminal text as a mechanism was that a run killed at a ceiling shows its last words wherever the axe fell. That objection dissolves twice over: the terminal record carries stop_reason: end_turn with subtype: success, so nothing terminated it — and there is no axe, because 55% of runs pass the same mark untouched.

Recorded rather than repaired, deliberately. Whether the budget should bind is a design question with real costs on both sides: enforcing it would have killed 168 first-attempt runs that went on to deliver, and leaving it advisory means the word budget promises something it does not do. What must not continue is the third state, where the surface accepts a figure, records it on every row, and neither enforces nor marks it.

The contamination, with its specimen. r-20260826T050636932486-reuse-map carries time_budget: 4m, wall_seconds: 633062.8 — 7.3 days — and worker_seconds: 140, against its own stamps of 05:06:39 → 05:08:59. A 140-second run holding a seven-day wall figure. Measured across the ledger: 328 rows carry a wall_seconds exceeding their elapsed time by more than half, the worst by 18,520×. Agreement with elapsed is 69% for wall_seconds and 98% for worker_seconds, and the specimen's own worker_seconds_source reads wall_fallback, so the bad value is what the fallback path produced.

What survives is the design point, unchanged. 244 runs exceeded a stated budget with no consequence. The surface accepts the figure, records it on every committed row, and neither enforces nor marks it. That third state is the defect and 23% is ample to establish it.

What does not survive is the operational advice, and it was the dangerous half. The retracted comment said a coordinator reading an overrun as trouble is reading the majority case. It is the minority case at 23%, and the typical run finishes in 39% of its budget. So an overrun is a genuine signal worth attending to, and a coordinator who treats one as notable is right rather than naive. Left standing, that sentence would have retrained two coordinators to ignore a working signal — which is a worse outcome than the unenforced budget it was describing.

And the methodological lesson is sharper than the figure. I did check for an artifact: I tested whether accumulation across resumes inflated the number, found 61 resumed rows, excluded them, and reported 168 first-attempt overruns as the resume-proof residue. That check was sound and aimed at the wrong suspect. The inflation was not accumulation across attempts; it was a stored field that is simply wrong on a third of rows, and excluding resumes could not touch it. Verifying against a second derivation of the same quantity would have caught it; verifying against a plausible confounder did not. The timestamps were available the whole time and share nothing with the field under suspicion.

reckon-ship · 2026-09-18T16:40:00Z

worker_seconds is safe to build on, and the disagreements all fall the harmless way. Asked by the peer coordinator before either of us starts trusting the field, on the correct grounds that 98% agreement is good and is not 100%.

MeasureResult
rows compared against completed_at − dispatched_at1,064
disagreeing by more than 10% or 60s11 (1.0%)
disagreements that overshoot elapsed0
range of the disagreements0.88× down to 0.12× — all under
source of every disagreeing rowstream_events

Every disagreement is worker time below wall elapsed, which is the expected direction — launch overhead and idle gaps between turns belong to the clock and not to the worker. The field never inflates. That is the property a calibration needs, and it is the opposite of wall_seconds, whose failures are all overshoot to the tune of 18,520×.

One thing the source breakdown settles that neither of us had assumed correctly. Across the ledger worker_seconds_source reads wall_fallback on 525 rows and stream_events on 456. So the fallback path is the majority source and is not the broken one — on the contaminated specimen it produced worker_seconds: 140, which is right, beside a wall_seconds of 633,062, which is not. The fallback is not copying the bad field. Whatever writes wall_seconds is a separate site from what fills worker_seconds when the stream is unavailable, and the investigation in flight should not assume they share a path.

Agreement between two readings of one field is not independent evidence

The methodological rule, which is the peer's phrasing and is the durable part of the whole episode. Two coordinators measured budget overruns independently, by different routes, on different row sets, and reached 55% and a comparable figure. Both were wrong, because both read wall_seconds. The disagreement that exposed it was luck: one of us happened to compute a worst case absurd enough to be disbelieved.

Had the two passes agreed, the contamination would have shipped carrying a corroboration stamp — two independent derivations, matching, both false. That is strictly worse than one unchecked number, because it converts a wrong figure into a confirmed one and closes the question. The check that works is a second derivation of the same quantity from a different input: here, timestamps, which share nothing with the field under suspicion and were available throughout.

This is the positive-control rule with the loophole named. Requiring evidence is not sufficient if the evidence and the claim are drawn from the same source — which is also why a test fixture quoting the string its guard greps for defeats the guard, and why a review record cannot vouch for its own completeness.

This is the plan's own thesis arriving in the gate rather than the display. The gate's claim is a true statement about a selection, read as a statement about the tree. The selection is derived from the node's write paths, which describe what the change touches and not what it reaches — and a derivation is reached by everything that consumes it.

The worker was not careless and that is the sharpest part. Its own follow_ons open with a scope-extension request, highest priority, naming the adjacent breakage in tests/test_roadmap_sprint_derivation.py:66 with the measurement beside it — 1 failed, 1 passed, the diff isolated to the derived label at one line. It knew its change reached past its fence, said so in the manifest, and asked. Its session ended before anyone answered, so the request sat in a field nothing reads at promotion time.

Four findings hold this row unpromoted, and the review's own score tracks them — 71 total, durability 12 and evidence 12, the lowest of the day: the invisible added failure; reckon/roadmap.py:967, where the suppression set {planned, open, active} includes planned so a stored-planned sprint with started members reports in-progress and no state_drift; reckon/roadmap.py:1962, where a new top-level open_sprints takes the name of an existing schedule-readiness field meaning a different set, so a payload reader cannot tell the buckets apart by name; and lint findings added against this repository's own delta rule, PT011 and W292 with three of five landed files unformatted.

The repair is not a bigger gate. Running everything on every node is what the focused-gate rule exists to prevent, and it would have cost this node an hour to catch one file. The gate needs to include what imports what the node changed, which is derivable rather than remembered — the same move as every other repair recorded here: compute the discriminator from a fact rather than from the author's account of their own scope.

§13 — A quiet fleet and a working one look identical, because nothing reports a wave

session-9e2222f55dd848415c74 · 2026-09-09T08:04:12Z

reuse map for all eleven measures: 11 rows, every reuse cell a real path:line, four serialisation lanes derived, and lane 4 named as prerequisite to the closing-line consumer

implement-terra-c · 2026-09-09T09:15:02Z

both dispatch surfaces accept a wave id; ordinary and shadow pointers persist the same wave; a shadow retains the supplied dispatching session while a distinct internal worktree identity preserves isolation; resume keeps its run id and redispatch mints a new run carrying its predecessor; attribution writes no contamination or exclusion field. Delta measured with the independently-confirmed deadlocking watcher test deselected and its cause recorded: 8 identical failure ids at base and head, zero added, 5 new passing cases

implement-terra-c · 2026-09-09T10:29:36Z

normal and shadow dispatches default to the latest non-empty live wave in their session, otherwise mint a new opaque id; explicit --wave wins; missing and empty legacy values are skipped so the three-population migration window is closed by the same commit that opens the default. 6 added cases, identical 8 failure ids at base and head with the known deadlock deselected and its cause recorded. Coordinator note: the dry-run payload carries no wave key, so a dry run cannot confirm the default and its silence is not evidence of failure

crew-attention · 2026-09-14T13:51:16.023Z

reuse map for the wave-lifecycle and runtime-gate sections: 17 measure rows, 3 satisfied / 8 partial / 6 absent, 33 file:line citations, per-section write-path sets with asserting tests named

reckon-ship · 2026-09-14T14:35:00+00:00

Prior-art phase complete: three reuse maps now cover all 35 unlanded measure rows across the seven pending sections, so implementation nodes have a map to cite. First promoted, gate passed against an independent scored review rather than its own author's check, no commit declared deliberately because the write path lies outside every git repository. Wave-lifecycle and runtime-gate map: 17 rows, 3 satisfied, 8 partial, 6 absent, 33 citations. Review total 79 of 100 - goal fidelity 19, evidence 19, scope discipline 19, fit 17, durability 5. The reviewer reproduced every sampled citation and all six absence greps independently, caught the same heading-versus-table row-count defect this coordinator caught, and caught one more that was missed: a retracted-mechanism paragraph attributed to the fourth measure row when it sits in the third row's cell. Two measures are already satisfied at the base and must not be redone - wave assignment on dispatch with the explicit-wins and empty-legacy negatives, and the token-denominated budget with the wall clock kept separately as a hang ceiling. One shared-file constraint governs the whole implementation wave: recovery.py appears in all three sections' write-path sets and ticker.py in two, so these sections cannot be dispatched concurrently and must be serialised. The live promotion of this very run reproduced the section it maps: its complete transition carried a full minute of wall, a minute of model time, 4.8M tokens and a rate, and its promoted transition 4 minutes later carried five empty cells.

crew-role-scope · 2026-09-14T14:28:35.663Z

independent review of the wave-lifecycle reuse map: 79/100 across five dimensions, two defects found, both verified by the coordinator before acceptance

reckon-ship · 2026-09-14T16:15:00+00:00

This session's own follower died at 16:04Z and the incident belongs here, because the follower is the signal this section is about. Cause, established by falsifier rather than by inspection: a commit added budget.coordinator_reserve_pct to the defaults file AND to the generated schema in the same commit, so every fresh process accepts it - verified, the key is present at that commit and absent at its parent, and the working tree is byte-identical to the committed file so nothing was regenerated. The follower had been running since 12:43Z holding the PRE-commit model in memory. Loading that older generated module directly and asking it shows the field absent, so the standing process rejected a defaults file that had since gained a key it could not know about. A schema change is safe for fresh invocations and unsafe for standing ones, and nothing tells a standing process that a config contract moved underneath it. HOW IT PRESENTED, which is the part this section owns. The crash surfaced only through the watch stream: crew list and crew dispatch worked throughout, and a peer's promotion succeeded through the very code path that killed the follower, because those are fresh processes. So the one long-lived process on the project was the only casualty and the fleet looked healthy from every command. The two signals that reached this coordinator were a dispatch refused with watcher-required - the arming guard working exactly as designed, before a worktree existed - and the host harness's own notice that the monitor exited non-zero. Neither came from reckon. A session whose harness does not report an exited monitor would have held a dead follower and read the resulting silence as a quiet fleet, which is this section's opening sentence. FOUR SESSIONS DIAGNOSED IT WRONG BEFORE ANYONE DIAGNOSED IT RIGHT, this one included: it was first read here as a repository breakage, then corrected to staleness, while a peer independently reported it as a missing regeneration from a grep truncated by head -6 against a count of 8 they did not reconcile. The instrument that settled it was loading the old model and asking whether the field existed - a positive control on the absence rather than an argument about it. Also recorded: this repository has no check that regenerating the flight schema produces no diff, so the failure mode the peer wrongly diagnosed is one nothing would catch if it did occur.

reckon-ship · 2026-09-14T20:50:00+00:00

A blind spot whose size is proportional to wave width, contributed by a peer coordinator and confirmed first-party here. THE FOLLOWER REPORTS ARRIVALS, NOT OUTCOMES. A dispatch refusal creates no run, so it emits no transition, so the stream is silent about it. Their instance: five triage partitions dispatched in a loop, one refused on per-member serialisation - the refusal correct and working as designed - and the pane showed five dispatched rows and nothing else. They caught it only by opening each dispatch result individually; had they trusted the pane, forty-two plans of an EXHAUSTIVE triage would have been silently uncovered, and the next chance to notice was a tiling check several nodes later. Measured in this session independently: 19 dispatched rows in the transition stream against roughly 25 dispatch attempts, so six refusals - watcher-required, member-in-flight twice, plan-unavailable, scope-conflict and unreconciled-runs - left no trace. No refusal-shaped state exists in the vocabulary at all, and the refusal strings appear nowhere on disk except in documents discussing them. Roughly a quarter of this coordinator's dispatch attempts are invisible to the surface built to report its fleet. THE SHAPE IS THE ONE THIS PLAN KEEPS FINDING, with a new twist: not a wrong answer and not a dropped field, but a question the stream cannot express, because a refusal genuinely has no run to hang a transition on. So the fix is not a synthetic row - inventing one may be worse than the gap, as they argued. What is owed is that refusals be countable somewhere a coordinator can compare against what it intended, and failing that, that the documentation say plainly that the stream cannot carry them. Harmless for a coordinator dispatching one node at a time, because the refusal is in the return value they are already reading; proportional to width for one dispatching a wave - and wave width is exactly what three sessions spent today trying to increase.

unknown · undated

Every status the crew tooling runs against a worker's worktree takes index.lock in that worktree, and a worker commit starting inside the window fails. Reported from a third session after one of its workers failed two commits in a row on a zero-byte, unheld lock and hit its two-failure fence. Verified here.

git status performs an optional index refresh that rewrites the index and holds the lock for the duration. Four call sites run it against trees the caller does not own, and the package contains no occurrence of --no-optional-locks or GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS anywhere:

dispatch.py:3993   status --porcelain=v1 --untracked-files=all --no-renames
routing.py:353     status --porcelain=v1 -z --untracked-files=all --no-renames
routing.py:414     status --porcelain
node.py:744        status --porcelain -- <paths>

With a watcher polling every few seconds across thirty-plus worktrees, the race is routine rather than exotic, and its symptom is a worker failing its own commit for a reason that has nothing to do with the worker.

The coordinator is a source too, and that is the part available to fix today. The untrust checks this plan's own discipline requires — a clean status --porcelain before believing a manifest — are run by hand against live workers' trees. Every one of those takes the same lock. So the verification routine that exists to catch a worker's defects can manufacture one, and it leaves no trace connecting the two: the coordinator sees a clean tree, the worker sees a failed commit, and nothing correlates them.

Two repairs, and the second needs no code. In the tooling, pass --no-optional-locks (or set GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0) on every status run against a tree the caller does not own — one node, but it needs dispatch.py, currently claimed, so it queues. In practice, every coordinator adds the flag to its own untrust commands immediately, because the cost is a keystroke and the alternative is breaking the run being inspected.

unknown · undated

The obvious repair for the lock race — set GIT_OPTIONAL_LOCKS=0 once at the git subprocess boundary — has no single place to go. There is no shared helper.

routing.py:242    _git()               subprocess.run(["git", *args], cwd=repo)   no env
node.py:650/670   _git_answer/_output  its own subprocess.run                    no env
dispatch.py:3948  _worktree_git_read   its own subprocess.run, timeout=10        no env

Three wrappers, no common boundary, and 32 subprocess.run( calls across six crew modules — resumption, routing, node, promotion, recovery, dispatch. That is almost certainly why the idiom is absent everywhere rather than missed at one site: there has never been one place to put it.

So the choice is not flag-versus-env. It is:

  • Env at the three worktree-reading wrappers — lands now, and leaves exactly the decay the env was meant to design out, since a fourth wrapper is what the history of six modules predicts.
  • One shared git-invocation helper carrying the env, with the status calls routed through it — what the reasoning actually asks for, and a refactor across six modules rather than four lines.

Recorded because the smaller version is the tempting one and it would let a coordinator report the race closed while the next added status reopens it. If the stop-gap is taken first for severity — the reporting session has now hit this twice in an hour on freshly dispatched nodes — it must be recorded as a stop-gap with the shared-helper node still open, not as the repair.

The general shape, which this plan has met several times today: a rule with nowhere to live decays into a rule nobody applies, and the absence of a boundary is the defect rather than the missing flag.

unknown · undated

The in_flight list every plan renders counts dead runs as running — 46% of its rows on this project, and the worst-affected plan is this one. Reported by another session and reproduced here with the project interpreter:

in_flight rows total         26
...with process_alive False  12   (46%)
   crew-observability-truth      7
   a-live-worker-can-be-reached  2
   history-persists-as-detail-washes-out  1
   roadmap-answers-both-shapes   1
   figures-are-allocated-by-topic-directory  1

mcp_views.in_flight_by_plan:986 takes crew.list_live() and groups by node.plan, copying out run_id, member, section and started_at. It consults neither liveness, nor disposition, nor classification. A live pointer survives all three, so it keeps rendering as in-flight work.

The fact it needs is in the record it is already holding. crew.list_live at runs.py:435 re-derives process_alive per record, including the pid-start-time comparison that defends against pid reuse, and its own comment states the principle: a read must not report a worker as live merely because the last observer did. The grouper iterates those records and drops the field. One filter, not new machinery — and the guard worth landing with it is a case asserting a process-dead pointer does not appear, because otherwise the two drift apart again in silence.

One caution, from the reporting session and worth keeping in the node: in_flight is load-bearing for coordinators deciding whether to dispatch, so an over-aggressive filter would hide genuinely running work. Filter on liveness only. A dispositioned or terminally-classified run can still have a live process, and the pid-start-time check already handles reuse.

Recorded with an admission: this is the surface this session has been reading all afternoon. Every read_plan returns an in_flight list, and it was used to judge what was running. On this plan, seven of those rows were dead.

### Shared files between the two sections — serialize or split

The two sets intersect on `reckon/crew/recovery.py`, `reckon/crew/promotion.py`,
`reckon/crew/ticker.py`, `reckon/cli.py` and `reckon/crew/dispatch.py`. Two nodes dispatched in
one wave over these sets would collide. Options, in order of preference:

1. One node owns both sections' shared files; the second node is dispatched only after the
   first lands, or
2. Split by section and assign each shared file to exactly one of the two nodes, with the other
   section's work in that file deferred to a follow-on node — in which case name in each brief
   which of the intersection files the node may touch.
3. A message-delivery path for §17 is the one piece with no existing home; it should get its
   own scope rather than landing inside a shared file.

A promotion's landing write silently discarded a concurrent edit_plan, and the version counter advanced as if nothing had been lost. Measured on this plan, on the comment directly above.

Sequence: edit_plan appended the composition finding and returned "Updated … to version 399". reckon crew complete was in flight for the-manifest-template-matches-the-reader and committed 426f6404. Afterwards:

CheckResult
plan-version meta399 — the number my write returned
my comment id, working treeabsent
my comment id, HEADabsent
the promotion's own landing commentpresent
the seven earlier comments from this sessionall present
git status on the planclean

So exactly one comment was lost — the one written inside the promotion's window — and the follow-up git commit reported nothing added to commit, because the working tree already matched a HEAD that did not contain the edit. Every surface agreed the write had succeeded: the tool returned a new version, the file carried that version, and git was clean.

The version-safe write is one-directional. edit_plan refuses on a stale expected_version; the landing path that promotion uses to append its own comment does not appear to be fenced by the same check, so it can read at one version and write back over a newer one while the counter still advances. A lost update that moves the version is undetectable by definition — the next reader sees a higher number and concludes it has the later state.

Recovered by re-applying the comment at 400 after diffing the surviving comment ids against what this session had written. That recovery only worked because the author was still in the session and still held the text; a plan edit lost this way to another session is unrecoverable and unreported.

index sprints:  S3 shipped, S4 done, S5 active(7 items), S6 done,

S18:            absent

roadmap(sprint="S18") answers anyway, reporting 6 plans, 1 completed, 16.7% lifecycle completion, critical path 10 hours — figures derived from the plans' own declarations rather than from any sprint record. So a caller asking for a sprint receives a membership nobody declared and nothing governs, and a sprint close would have nothing to close.

It also explains three plan-sprint-missing-item findings verbatim: "declares sprint S18 but is absent from its items" is what the check emits when the item list it consults does not exist. The three plans are not misfiled.

This is the plan's own subject arriving one layer up. roadmap(sprint=<id>) reads like a sprint query and is a scan of five meta tags; the difference is invisible because the answer is well-formed and specific. The repair belongs to roadmap-answers-both-shapes, whose subject is exactly what that surface should answer — either the sprint is resolved against the index and an unknown id refuses, or the derived membership is labelled as derived.

Two things this does not touch, recorded so the boundary is clear: every node promoted under the name landed against a real plan with real state, and the ledger rows carry their own commits and evidence, so nothing depended on the sprint existing. And active_sprint_id reads S17 while S5 is the only sprint whose status is active — a second inconsistency in the same record, left unrepaired here because inventing either answer would paper over it.

Retraction of the comment above: S18 exists, is richly authored, and always has. I read a stale artifact and asserted an absence from it.

The project uses distributed state. compose_project_state yields sixteen sprints, S3 through S18, and the S18 record carries a theme ("A signal reports what it measures"), status planned, version 6, a capacity of 19 worker-hours, a full description and a detailed handoff summary. docs/state/reckon/index.json holds eight sprints, has not been modified since 2026-09-04, and is not the store this project reads — it is a legacy-index artifact that the distributed path does not consult.

The three plan-sprint-missing-item findings were precise and my reading inverted them. S18's item list exists and holds two members, crew-observability-truth and roadmap-answers-both-shapes. Five plans declare plan-sprint: S18. So three plans genuinely declare the sprint and are absent from its members — exactly what the finding said. I read "absent from its items" as "the item list does not exist" and went looking for a missing sprint instead of three missing memberships.

What makes this the worst instance of the day is that the contradicting evidence was already in hand. A sprint-scoped roadmap read had answered with six plans, a completion percentage and a critical path. I explained that away as derivation from meta tags rather than treating it as the surface reporting a real sprint. An answer I could not account for was reasoned into agreement with my hypothesis instead of being allowed to refute it.

The rule that would have caught it is the one already recorded on this plan and applied correctly four times today: read the surface, not the raw store. crew list over the pointer files, _routing_outcome_exclusion over measurement_exclusion_reason, the composed event over a grep of the renderer — and then index.json over compose_project_state, which is the same error with the surface and the store swapped.

The exclusion-counted-as-input refusal turned out to have two causes, and separating them took a peer failing to reproduce it. They ran the same experiment and got no refusal at all, because the fit fields appear only on a refusal payload and nothing they could compose came near their window. Their lane read 1,016,576 usable input tokens; mine read 172,800, same host, same backend, same hour. Traced through the recorded runs: every clive dispatch before 12:49Z today carries 1,016,576 and every one from 12:49Z carries 172,800, and the host config layer declaring it has an mtime of 12:51:31Z - it was edited while this wave was dispatching. So the declared window fell by a factor of 5.9 mid-wave with nothing announcing it, and the launcher's own banner still advertises the larger figure. Two separate defects, and only the second was visible to one observer: a node's fit estimate counts paths named as exclusions, which is true at any window, and the window it is measured against disagreed with the lane, which is what made a fitting node refuse. Recorded here rather than repaired because the value sits in a shared host layer this plan does not own. The general shape is this plan's own subject arriving in the routing config: a stored number, a machine that says otherwise, and a refusal computed from the record.

CORRECTION to the comment above, within the hour, from a third coordinator: it has the direction wrong and the entry above should be read through this one. The window change is owned and fully documented. The serve now enforces a 204,800-token cap at the engine and the launcher reserves 32,000 for output, so 172,800 is what the server will accept; 1,016,576 was the checkpoint's full native window and became an overstatement the moment the cap landed, with nodes sized against it admitted and then refused by the serve with HTTP 400. The config carries all of this in a dated comment block immediately above the backend definition, together with the script that re-derives the figure and a warning that it goes stale whenever the deployment's context length moves. Nothing was unannounced. This reading missed it by grepping from the backend key downward and never seeing the block above, which is this plan's own aperture defect committed by its coordinator: an instrument aimed one block below the answer returns a confident absence indistinguishable from a real one. The surviving finding inverts and is worth more than the one it replaces. The lane's launch banner still advertises 1,016,576 on every stderr, including runs dispatched after the cap, so the stale surface is the launcher describing the checkpoint it loaded rather than the serve that is answering - the same trap recorded one section over, where a healthy banner printed to the end of runs the serve was refusing. A figure a reader trusts and the engine rejects is the exact shape of this plan. The exclusion-counted-as-input measure is unaffected and now matters more, because the real window is small and constrained rather than generous: 182,258 of the 232,650 estimated tokens were paths the node was told not to open, against a genuine 172,800 ceiling.

reckon-ship · 2026-09-14T14:00:00+00:00

The surviving half of the window finding, corrected in mechanism and handed to the plan that owns it. The utilisation denominator is not a constant: there is no 200,000 anywhere in this source. Verified by reading it - reckon/_backends.py:1147 takes contextWindow from the stream's own per-model usage entries, keeps the minimum across models on the stated ground that a shared prompt overflows the smallest first, passes it as input_budget_tokens at :1176, and :337 divides peak input by it. The local lane speaks a passthrough dialect, so what lands on every one of its rows is the CLIENT's declared window rather than the serving deployment's - the same stream also announces a canonical model that is not the one running. That makes it the inherited-price defect one field over: this lane already totals the highest dollar figure of any backend by inheriting an unrelated provider's per-token rates, and this is the same inheritance in a different field. The denominator is the quieter of the pair, because a cost table ranking free hardware as the dearest looks absurd on sight while 71.0 percent of a context window looks exactly like a measurement. The binding remedy belongs to a-lane-can-say-where-it-stands, which has taken it as a section: a utilisation names the window it divided by and takes that window from the authority that enforces it, returning unknown rather than splitting the difference when the client and the configured lane disagree. Not restated here beyond the cross-reference, because one rule in two plans is how two statements of it begin to drift.

A sharper instance of two surfaces disagreeing about what is permitted, measured on this plan's own fleet at 13:53Z, and this one is a cycle rather than a contradiction. A run that completes with a manifest now classifies scoring, and the recovery surface's next action is to dispatch its independent review. That same run is also an unreconciled run, and once it passes the five-minute grace, dispatch refuses ALL new work for the session with unreconciled-runs, listing each blocking run beside the command that resolves it. The command it printed for the blocking run was, character for character, the review dispatch being attempted - the refusal quoted the attempt back as its own remedy. So the only exit is to waive the very run the new node exists to service, with a flag whose name says the backlog is being left deliberately when in fact it is being cleared. Worth stating as its own shape: the earlier instance had one surface prescribing what another refused, which a reader can resolve by picking a side; here neither side is wrong and the pair has no fixed point. A gate that admits a run into a state only reachable by a dispatch, while a fence refuses dispatches because the run is in that state, is a deadlock however correct each half is alone. The scoring state should not count toward the unreconciled backlog that gates its own review, or the review dispatch should be exempt from the fence. Recorded with the waiver on run r-20260914T135359878507. A refusal that names a true fact about the wrong thing, hit twice today and diagnosable only because it was hit twice. Promotion writes TWO tracked files - the ledger row and an idempotent landing comment appended to the plan HTML by _record_landing_comment at promotion.py:1083 - and commits neither. The next dispatch then reads the plan at its base revision, finds the file dirty, and refuses plan-unavailable naming the section. The section is fine. The operator learns about promotion's side effect from a later verb, in a message about a plan, minutes after the verb that caused it returned success. REORDERING DOES NOT FIX IT and the question is worth answering precisely: the defect is not the sequence of the two writes but that a tool writes tracked files and leaves the caller holding uncommitted state with no signal. Either order leaves the tree dirty. Three properties would each fix it, and they are not equal. Committing what it writes is the strongest - promotion already knows the run, the commit and the gate, and a verb that mutates two tracked stores atomically also closes the interruption window its own docstring worries about between the ledger append and the pointer removal. Refusing to run against a dirty plan is the cheapest and is symmetrical with the dispatch refusal, bounding the dirty window to one landing and reporting at the verb that causes it. Returning the comment as data for the coordinator to apply is the most orthodox, since the landing beat is already mandatory, but it removes a safety net deliberately built against a coordinator that skips the beat - which is the silent-bypass failure this repository's own guidance was written after, so it trades a known hazard for an older one. NOTE THE DOUBLE WRITE EITHER WAY: the plan is written once by the tool and once by the coordinator's mandatory landing beat, so every landing produces two comments on one section. That duplication is invisible until someone reads a section's comment list and finds the same landing described twice in two voices.

That removes the hanging side effect recorded above, where an operator learned about promotion's write from a LATER verb - a dispatch refusing plan-unavailable and naming a section that was fine - minutes after the causing verb returned success. It also narrows the mis-attribution window measured earlier today, where one commit from this session carried 37 rows of which 29 belonged to three other coordinators' plans: a landing now commits at the moment it happens rather than whenever someone next remembers. ONE RESIDUAL, NAMED RATHER THAN DISCOVERED LATER. The test suite covers an unrelated DIRTY file and asserts it stays uncommitted; it does not cover a pre-STAGED one, and dirty is not staged. The window is the gap between a peer's git add and its git commit, which is sub-second where those are one command and unbounded where they are not. The remedy is one flag: committing the named paths only, which git treats as commit-only regardless of index state. Recorded as a follow-on rather than held against the landing, because the change is strictly better than the state it replaces and the residual is narrower than the defect it fixes - but it is the same defect one layer in, and this plan should not let that pass unnamed twice in one day.

THE CHECK THAT VERIFIES THE FIX IS ITSELF THE DEFECT, and four sessions were misled by it today including this one. Reported by a peer coordinator who measured it in one beat, reproduced here independently. Node-contract validation stops at the first failing property, so a node that fails demonstrable never reaches the scope computation and the landing grant is never applied. Same role, same section, same write path, same spec level, varying only the done-when:

weak   ("it works")                findings ['demonstrable']       node.write_paths 1
strong ("...asserts 3 cases...")   findings ['scoped','scoped']    node.write_paths 3

This session was the first of the four and did not notice. The opening dry-run of the session returned findings: ['demonstrable']; the done-when was strengthened, and only then did the two scoped findings appear. That was recorded at the time as fixed the measure, then found the scope defect. The true sequence is that the short-circuit concealed the scope defect from the first probe and the discovery was luck. Three other sessions reached the opposite conclusion from the same behaviour — that the read-only regression was already fixed — one from weak probes, one from a placeholder goal, and one from a write-path count that two coordinators then spent several rounds failing to account for.

The misleading value is the path count, not the verdict. A weak done-when can never report clean, because it always fails demonstrable; nobody reads validation true, zero findings off one. What misleads is write_paths: 1 — a reader sees a single declared path, concludes the grant is no longer being appended, and calls the regression fixed. So the defect is not that validation stops early; it is that it emits a partial node as though it were a complete one. That is the same shape this plan already records for a manifest returning eight keys and no status: a partial result is worse than a refusal because it manufactures a plausible wrong answer, and plausible wrong answers are the ones that survive review.

The requirement, in the peer's own framing. Report every failing property rather than stopping at the first, so this class cannot be made unmeasurable by accident. The argument for it is specific rather than general: a dry-run probe is exactly how anyone verifies the landing-grant repair has landed, and today a sloppy probe reports success. Both defects share one cause — a check that never runs — which is why the repair and the probe that confirms the repair must not be the same node's work.

reckon-ship · 2026-09-15T06:32:00Z

REFINEMENT TO THE REQUIREMENT ABOVE, and it changes what the node must build. The comment above names report every failing property rather than stopping at the first as the fix. The peer who found the defect corrected that after reading this framing back, and the correction is right: a node that never reached grant computation must not report a write-path list at all. Reporting a truthful-looking short list is the deception; enumerating every failing property is the second half, not the whole.

The distinction matters because the two repairs have different failure modes. Enumerating properties alone still emits write_paths: 1 beside the extra findings, so a reader skimming the path count draws the same wrong inference with more text around it. Suppressing the list — absent, not short — makes the incomplete computation unreadable as a complete one, which is the only thing that stops the inference. Do both, in that order of importance.

Stated in one sentence with its sibling, because they are one defect in two surfaces: a node whose scope was never computed and a manifest returning eight keys with no status both manufacture a plausible answer from an incomplete computation, and a plausible wrong answer is worse than a refusal because nothing prompts a second look.

The dispatch template adds both paths to every node on a plan, because every node records its own landing. Dispatch then accepts the overlap without complaint — correctly, since those two files are append-only in practice and the landing beat is serialized by the coordinator. The consequence is that a plan with two live nodes can never have a parked node auto-resumed. Manual crew resume goes through, so the parked work is recoverable by a coordinator who notices; nothing recovers it on its own. With 6 of 18 live plans already in that state, the sweep is disabled for exactly the plans busy enough to need it.

The repair is a shared understanding rather than a threshold: either the plan and evidence HTML are exempt from the collision check, or they are declared append-only and the check reads that. Two components currently disagree about whether the same two paths are exclusive, and only one of them refuses.

A review dispatch named a destination keyed to a run id that does not exist, and every check downstream passed. The reviewer ran, read the correct commits, scored 99, found a real defect — and wrote its record where nothing will ever look for it, while its subject correctly reported awaiting review.

dispatched --write-path  reviews/reckon/r-20260915T084936000000-a-commit-identifier-…json
actual run               r-20260915T090617465885-a-commit-identifier-…
run directory for 084936000000   does not exist

The trailing zeros are the tell: a real run id carries microsecond precision. But the value is well formed in every respect a reader checks — correct prefix, correct node suffix, correct length, plausible date — and --write-path accepts any string. The reviewer's own reviewed_commit is d7a7dc52 against base 3332b9d3, which are the right commits, so the work was sound and only its address was fiction.

This is the identifier-shaped member of the family the rest of this plan documents, and the first instance where the coordinator originated the bad value rather than misreading an existing one. The repo already carries the rule for commits — verify existence, not shape, git rev-parse --verify <sha>^{commit} — and there is no counterpart for a run id in a dispatch path. A dispatch that resolved its --write-path against the live pointer set would have refused this in one comparison.

Disposed by re-dispatching rather than renaming the file. A copy and one edited field would have been cheaper, and it would have made the coordinator the author of the review evidence that gates its own promotion — which is the arrangement §21 exists to prevent, wearing a different hat. One worker on an unmetered lane is the cheaper thing to spend. The orphaned record stays on disk as corroboration.

the-project-watch-test-terminates · 2026-09-28T07:25:00Z

MEASURE 2'S RECORDED CAUSE IS REFUTED, AND THE TEST IS REPAIRED IN tests/test_crew.py ALONE. The measure says this test deadlocks, “its main thread joining while its worker stays inside the watch loop in reckon/crew/runs.py”. Measured at base: the watch reaches its own controlled sleeper 0.140 s after the watcher thread starts, the main thread's watch-armed dispatch returns at 5.303 s, and the AssertionError is raised by the test's own sleeper at 5 s — tests/test_crew.py:1837: assert release.wait(timeout=5). Both halves of the recorded cause have the direction wrong, and that is why the failure presented as a hang: the traceback (runs.py:3247: in watch → test_crew.py:1837) surfaces at the main thread's watcher.result(), so it names the watch as the slow party while the slow party is the dispatch and the deadline is the test's. The dispatch's 5.3 s is ordinary work on GPFS, profiled rather than assumed: 33 subprocess.run calls totalling 3.591 s (git spawns at ~0.48 s here against ~0.09 s in /tmp), a 1.256 s _coordinator_accounting glob over 2,631 lexists calls, 1.296 s of lstat traffic across 7,337 calls. Nothing waits on a lock and reckon/crew/ticker.py is not on this path. The verdict is speed-dependent, which is the proof that the deadline is the defect: in the base full-file census this test passed inside a process already ~200 tests warm, while isolated it failed 3 of 3 (7.15 / 6.95 / 7.10 s). The repair: the sleeper becomes pure synchronisation (release.wait(), no deadline); the 5 s bounds move onto the subjects they measure (the watch reaching its sleeper, which needs 0.140 s; and a join plus assert not watcher.is_alive() after the release, so a genuinely stuck watch fails by name in ~5 s instead of hanging the suite); the watcher's exception is captured and re-raised on the test thread; release.set() sits in a finally so no path strands the watch. No timeout lengthened, nothing deselected, and every assertion in the test still runs. Head gate 3 consecutive runs, 6.45 / 5.80 / 5.56 s, exit 0 each; base isolated arm red 3 of 3 with the same assertion; negative control declared before it ran (“reintroduce the identified cause in a scratch copy; the watch-armed first-dispatch test must fail on release.wait”) reproduced with the base revision's test file as the scratch module against the change's own source: assert False at /tmp/negctl/tests/test_crew.py:1837, exit 1. Two things handed back rather than absorbed. The measure's other evidence — a pair terminated at exit 143 and the same test past 90 s — did not reproduce here (nothing in this node's 12 arms exceeded 7.7 s), so either those were this cause under heavier load or there is a second cause this node did not reach; a coordinator who reproduces a >90 s hang should treat it as a new node rather than as unfinished work here. And the measure's own wording should be corrected by its owner, since a reader planning against “deadlocks... inside the watch loop” will look in runs.py and find nothing. Full arms, logs and the figure: docs/evidence/archive/crew-observability-truth-landed.html#watch-test-deadline-lands-on-the-dispatch.

A base delta gate therefore always completes, and the hang shows in the base arm's failure ids like any other red. Second, the census itself measured the one recorded deadlock, test_first_dispatch_proceeds_with_a_freshly_armed_project_watch, passing in 7.00 s, so no non-completing test is known to register. A registry with no entry and a bound that already converts a hang into a failure would be machinery with nothing to hold.

Disposition of all eight census items: dry-run admission (d7efb0a57), fit-estimate exclusion (c952174a7), two done-when lints and a warning (0a1708c8f), widen refusal (8b2bf60c5), and the scopes-view evaluated state (6a4bbe27c) landed. The wave-assignment item was met by the dry-run change. This item is superseded by the per-test bound. Reopen it if a test is found that the 300 s bound does not end, such as one that hangs in collection or in a session fixture.

# Reuse map — dispatch-refusal surface (§15) and manifest-classification surface (§16)

Plan: `reckon:crew-observability-truth`, sections 15 and 16. Surveyed at base revision
**5384182** (`git rev-parse HEAD` in the assigned worktree), read-only. Verdict per
measure row: `satisfied` / `partial` / `absent`, each satisfied or partial verdict with a
`file:line` citation, plus a proposed exclusive write-path set per section with the test
files that assert on each source.

Measure rows found: **9** — 6 in §15's table, 3 in §16's table. The gate expected 9.

---

## §15 — Dispatch's refusal surface

### 15.1 A dry run names what it did not check — **satisfied**

The payload evaluates live path claims and names the owning run, which is the second half
of the measure's either/or (it chose "evaluates them and names the owning run" rather than
"states they were not evaluated").

- `reckon/cli.py:1132` passes `report_live_conflicts=True` on the `crew dispatch --dry-run`
  path (cli.py:1121-1168), which reuses the *same* `plan_dispatch` used by the real
  dispatch rather than a second implementation.
- `reckon/crew/dispatch.py:2026-2035` populates `resolution.live_conflicts` via
  `_live_conflict_rows` only when the verdict is ok — a clean dry run carries the conflict
  list rather than hiding the fact that it checked.
- `reckon/crew/dispatch.py:895-931` `_live_conflict_rows` builds the rows naming
  `run_id`, `node`, `claimed_path`, `paths`, and `project` for a cross-project claim; it
  paths through the same `_scopes_overlap` / `_candidate_scope_entries` logic as the
  dispatch-time refusal `_raise_repository_scope_conflict` (dispatch.py:934-980), so a
  conflict the dry run reports is one dispatch would raise — the disregard mechanism is
  shared (non-binding claims are skipped in both, recorded in `disregarded`/`warnings`).
- Asserted both ways: `tests/test_crew_dryrun.py:151-175` (held claim → `live_conflicts`
  names `run_id`/`node`, validation stays `ok`); :177-189 (disjoint claim → `live_conflicts
  == []`); :192-239 (declared derivation → conflict reported). The disregard negative is
  asserted on the dispatch side at `tests/test_crew_cross_project_claims.py:373-403`.

Residual: the payload does not enumerate the remaining record-construction fields it never
evaluates (the §15 prose names the wave id), and no test asserts the dry-run conflict list
equals the dispatch refusal list element-for-element — only that each conflict the dry run
reports is a real one.

### 15.2 A delta gate that cannot complete is named before it is demanded — **absent**

Both halves are unmet, and the defect reproduces at this revision.

- The non-completing test is still live and still not deselected:
  `tests/test_crew.py:1806` `test_first_dispatch_proceeds_with_a_freshly_armed_project_watch`.
  **Measured at base 5384182: the single test did not complete within 130 s (timeout killed
  it, exit 124)** — the pre-existing deadlock persists (worker inside the watch loop in
  `reckon/crew/runs.py`, main thread joining in the `ThreadPoolExecutor.__exit__` without a
  bound).
- No dispatch surface names a file carrying a non-completing test when a done-when demands a
  delta over it. Grep for `non_completing|deselect|deadlock` over `reckon/crew/*.py`,
  `reckon/cli.py`, `tests/conftest.py` returns no mechanism.

Reusable surface for the fix: the advisory-report shape is established by
`_done_when_plan_overlap_warning` (`reckon/crew/dispatch.py:255-283`) — quoted, advisory,
and deliberately unable to break a dispatch. A "this file's delta cannot be taken" naming
the offending test belongs beside it or as a `demonstrable` finding in `validate_node`
(`reckon/crew/node.py:491`).

### 15.3 A falsifier states agreement, not a range, wherever a second measurement exists — **absent**

No dispatch-time check distinguishes a range-shaped falsifier from an agreement-shaped one.
The nearest existing surface is the done-when wording validator: the `demonstrable`
property demands an evidence signal and refuses subjective predicates
(`reckon/crew/node.py:533-556`, `_EVIDENCE_SIGNALS` at node.py:101-105,
`_SUBJECTIVE_PREDICATE` at node.py:128-134). Nothing in it inspects a falsifier for
"within X%…Y%" range phrasing versus an independent measurement, so a range-only done-when
passes today.

### 15.4 A done-when satisfiable by absence is refused at dispatch — **partial**

The refusal machinery and the property are in place; the specific escape hatch is not
detected.

- `reckon/crew/node.py:551-556`: a done-when with no evidence signal is refused as a
  `demonstrable` finding at dispatch (validation is binding in `dispatch`, node.py:501-503).
- The trap construction is not covered: a measure reading "measured **or explicitly
  unmeasured**" still carries an evidence signal and passes; nothing scans for the
  absence-escape or asserts corpus coverage. The `_EVIDENCE_SIGNALS` regex (node.py:101-105)
  matches independent of any editorial escape clause.

### 15.5 A done-when demanding absolute green is refused at dispatch — **partial**

Same surface, same shape as 15.4.

- `reckon/crew/node.py:101-105`: `_EVIDENCE_SIGNALS` counts `\bexit\b` and `\bpasses\b` as
  *positive* evidence — so "the suite exits zero" validates today, and no check reads a base
  failure count to quote back what the coordinator just demanded. The measure's "[refused],
  or accepted with the base failure count quoted back" therefore has no dispatch half.
- The "report, never refuse" precedent for a done-when-quality matter exists at
  `_done_when_plan_overlap_warning` (`reckon/crew/dispatch.py:255-283`).

### 15.6 Granting a scope extension is a command — **absent**

No verb records an additional exclusive path on a live run.

- The only scope verb is `--scope-changed` on `crew complete` (`reckon/cli.py:2651-2655`,
  threaded through `reckon/crew/promotion.py:1412,2108`); it annotates that scope moved and
  deliberately does not waive the write-scope validator — the "answers a later and different
  question" gap §15 names.
- `crew resume` (`reckon/cli.py:2444-2448`) accepts `--advice/--backend/--reason/--print-only`
  only; there is no write-path option.
- Reusable half: the peer-collision detector a grant verb must consult already exists as
  `_claimed_write_paths` (`reckon/crew/resumption.py:495-519`, exercised by `_claim_conflicts`
  at resumption.py:937) — the exact "refuses when a peer holds that path" predicate. The
  promoted-row carry would reuse the `scope_changed` plumbing in
  `reckon/crew/promotion.py:1412/2108` and the ledger read the measure demands
  ("read off the committed record rather than the pointer").

---

## §16 — Manifest classification

### 16.1 A complete manifest is never classified abandoned — **absent** (reproduces)

Confirmed at base with a positive reproduction, not by reading:

```
status: complete
- reckon/cli.py: added the refusal
- tests/test_cli.py: five new cases
```
parses to `status = "complete, reckon/cli.py: added the refusal, tests/test_cli.py: five new cases"`
and `manifest_status_is_terminal(...)` returns `False` (vocabulary `{"blocked","complete","failed"}`).

Chain, all live at 5384182:
- The join: `reckon/crew/reports.py:129-131` — a column-0 bullet line after any `key:` line
  appends to that key, so prose bullets beneath `status:` run the value on (ready made into
  `_coerce_list_field`-style splitting elsewhere, but never re-parsed into the terminal check).
- The status feed: `reckon/crew/recovery.py:1172-1177` takes the run-on verbatim as
  `manifest_status` (it is not a template, so it is not blanked).
- The misclassification: the run-on falls through every terminal arm to the abandoned arm
  `reckon/crew/recovery.py:1614-1641`, whose `delivery` names it at :1628
  (`"the manifest status ... is not usable"`) and whose action at :1638-1640 advises
  *inspect the worktree and redispatch if needed* — exactly the "redo it" a complete run must
  never receive. The §16 prose premise (a `complete` manifest becomes
  `completed_unpromoted`) is otherwise honored by `manifest_status_is_terminal`
  (`recovery.py:207-212`) and the terminal vocabulary at `recovery.py:72-76`; the parser
  defeats the mapping before the classifier ever sees a clean value.

### 16.2 The fixture is the failing shape, not the shape that looks like it — **absent**

Scanned every `tests/*.py` fixture for the failing shape (bullets at column 0 directly under
`status:`): **zero** occurrences. The refuted hypothesis (blank-line count) is recorded in
the plan §16 itself — the fix node must not re-test it. The nearest fixtures are the
bracketed-list shape: `tests/test_manifest_parse_format.py:45` and
`tests/test_manifest_nested_keys.py:16-24` — the shape that passes while reproducing nothing.

### 16.3 Two fields disagreeing is the cheapest detector — **absent**

Reproduction on the same fixture: `commits` parses cleanly to a single sha
`['5384182abc14ee26159c13769f3eadb81ccf296c']` while `status` is the run-on above
(`reckon/crew/recovery.py:1188` reads `manifest_commits` from the same parsed doc). No check
asserts that a terminal phase carrying a parsed commit beside an unusable status is never
classified `abandoned`; no test covers the combination §16 names as its cheap detector.

---

## Proposed exclusive write-path sets

### §15 — dispatch-refusal surface

| Write path | Test files that assert on it |
|---|---|
| `reckon/crew/dispatch.py` (dry-run conflict reporting, live-conflict rows, the refusal raise, advisory done-when warnings) | `tests/test_crew_dryrun.py`, `tests/test_crew_dispatch_guard.py`, `tests/test_crew_routing_visibility.py`, `tests/test_crew_refusal_visibility.py`, `tests/test_crew_cross_project_claims.py` |
| `reckon/crew/node.py` (the eight-node-contract validation, `_EVIDENCE_SIGNALS`, `_SUBJECTIVE_PREDICATE`, `_scopes_overlap`) | `tests/test_crew.py` (validate_node/demonstrable properties), `tests/test_role_write_scope.py`, `tests/test_crew_node.py` |
| `reckon/crew/resumption.py` (`_claimed_write_paths`/`_claim_conflicts` — the grant verb's collision predicate) | `tests/test_crew_recover.py` |
| `reckon/crew/promotion.py` (`scope_changed` carry onto the promoted row) | `tests/test_crew_promotion_scope.py`, `tests/test_ledger.py` |
| `reckon/cli.py` (the grant verb, `--scope-changed`, `--dry-run` flag plumbing) | `tests/test_crew.py`, `tests/test_crew_refusal_visibility.py`, `tests/test_crew_dryrun.py` |
| `tests/test_crew.py` (fix-or-deselect the non-completing watch test at :1806; a deselection must state its cause per §15) | `tests/test_crew.py` — the watch test asserts on `reckon/crew/runs.py`'s watch loop, so if the deadlock is *fixed*, `reckon/crew/runs.py` joins this set and `tests/test_crew.py` stays the asserting file |

### §16 — manifest-classification surface

| Write path | Test files that assert on it |
|---|---|
| `reckon/crew/reports.py` (`_parse_text_manifest` — stop appending prose bullets to a scalar key, or split the joined value before the terminal check) | `tests/test_manifest_parse_format.py`, `tests/test_manifest_nested_keys.py` |
| `reckon/crew/recovery.py` (classifier's status consumption at :1172-1177, the abandoned arms at :1614-1641/1664-1674, and the new two-fields detector) | `tests/test_a_rewritten_terminal_manifest_transitions.py`, `tests/test_crew_finished_display.py`, `tests/test_crew_recover.py` |
| the new fixture-bearing test (16.2: value-continuing bullets under `status:`, not the blank-line hypothesis) | itself, plus the two report tests above |

---

## Notes for the fix nodes

- 15.2's "says so" half can reuse `_done_when_plan_overlap_warning`'s advisory shape so it
  quotes the offending test and the file it is demanded over; the *deadlock fix* half belongs
  in `reckon/crew/runs.py` (the watch loop the worker never leaves) — measured present at
  base, so a repair node must first show the same exit-124 reproduction.
- 15.4/15.5 both land in `validate_node`'s `demonstrable` property
  (`reckon/crew/node.py:533-556`), which is already the dispatch-time refusal the measures
  call for; 15.5 additionally needs the base-revision failure count read, whose pattern the
  delta-policy text already establishes.
- 15.6 is a new CLI verb with the collision predicate already built
  (`resumption.py:495-519`) and the promotion carry already plumbed (`promotion.py:1412`,
  `:2108`) — the missing surface is the verb and the dispatch-side wiring, not the rule.
- 16.1's fix is a parse-boundary decision (reports.py:129-131), not a classifier change; the
  classifier's abandoned arms stay correct once it sees a clean terminal value. Verify the
  guarded thing by making a `status: complete` + bullets manifest classify *not*-abandoned
  (current: abandoned, shown above).
