THE FOURTH INSTANCE OF THE CONTRACT-FENCE DISAGREEMENT, and the one that explains why this plan keeps finding unguarded records. Raised by the lead as a question — should a review or investigate worker not be able to create a research document? — and measured rather than reasoned about. It cannot. Every writable grant on the read-only tier lies outside the repository:

write path 'docs/research/gc-at-scale-prior-art.html' is unreachable in resolved
sandbox tier 'read-only'; writable grants:
  ~/.config/reckon/crew/reports
  ~/.config/reckon/crew/reviews
  ~/.config/reckon/crew/runs/<this run>
  /run/user/39486

The ratio is the finding. 638 files have accumulated in the crew reports directory, 40 of them reuse maps, against 15 tracked files in docs/research/. So substantially all investigative output this project has produced is machine-local, unversioned, outside git, invisible to any other checkout, and reapable by the same cleanup that clears run directories. Not because anyone chose that — because the only roles that produce investigation are fenced out of the only place the repository's own rules say such documents belong. The project's guidance is explicit that RCAs, incident reports and explainers are HTML under docs/; the tier makes that unreachable for the roles that write them.

This plan already named the defect one level up and did not see the cause. §21 records that reviewers raised an unguarded record that nothing reads against the reuse maps, and that the review store is six records, unversioned, machine-local. Both were read as storage choices to be corrected per-artifact. They are not choices at all: they are what the sandbox tier forces, and any future scout or reviewer will reproduce them exactly. A finding that recurs in every instance of a class is a property of the mechanism, not of the instances.

Why the obvious fix is wrong, and what the right one is. The read-only tier exists so a reader cannot edit the code it is grading, and that purpose is sound — widening the tier to the worktree would destroy it. But docs/research/ is not the code under grading. The tier is denying a category it has no reason to deny, because it is keyed on inside or outside the repository when the property it wants is source and tests, or not. The repair is to grant a read-only role its declared paths under the documentation tree while continuing to refuse source and tests — which is the same shape as the two disagreements already recorded against this section: a fence and a contract that answer different questions about what a role may write.

It also silently weakens the prior-art rule. A scout's reuse map is required to be cited by the nodes that follow it, and citation across sessions requires the map to be readable from a checkout. Today it is readable only on the machine that produced it, so the requirement is satisfiable in the session that dispatches the scout and unenforceable afterwards — which is why the four maps this plan cites are consulted by hand rather than linked from the evidence record.

SIXTH CONTRACT-VERSUS-FENCE INSTANCE, AND THE FIRST ENTIRELY INSIDE ONE PROMPT. Reported by a peer coordinator whose worker blocked cleanly rather than racing, and reproduced here from a live dispatch payload. The worker is handed both of these:

CONTRACT — LANDING YOUR RECORD
  Append your landing record to your own section of the plan and your evidence
  anchor to the cumulative evidence record; both live in this worktree...

PEER SCOPES
  a-second-key-on-a-manifest-line-is-reported:
      docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html
      docs/evidence/archive/crew-observability-truth-landed.html

Measured on this session's own dispatch: 25 peer entries, and every same-plan peer discloses exactly those two paths as its claim. So the prompt instructs the worker to append to a file and, forty lines later, tells it the file belongs to somebody else. A careful worker blocks with a NEEDS-HELP, which is what the peer's node did and the right call on the information it had.

The disclosure is simply false, and that is what makes this fixable rather than a trade-off. The landing paths were deliberately exempted from the exclusive-claim refusal when the grant landed, on the stated reasoning that every node on one plan appends to the same two files and git merge reconciles the appends — which is true and was demonstrated twice today, once by five concurrent runs of this session holding the same plan file and dispatching normally, and once by a worker-authored record merging clean against ten intervening commits. A path that is shared by design is not an exclusive claim, so listing it under a peer's exclusive scope states the opposite of the rule the dispatcher is following.

The repair is to stop disclosing the shared landing paths as peer claims, rather than to explain them in the contract. Explaining would leave a worker reconciling two true statements at run time, every run; excluding them makes the peer-scope block mean one thing again — these paths are exclusively someone else's. The peer's proposed test (two concurrent nodes, same plan, disjoint write paths, must both dispatch) already passes and is not the falsifier: dispatch admits them today. The assertion that fails is on the composed prompt — a peer's disclosed scope must not contain the plan or evidence path that this node is simultaneously instructed to append to.

Why this was invisible to the session that introduced it. The grant's own tests proved the two things its author checked — that a second dispatch on the same plan is admitted, and that promotion accepts a run that wrote both paths. Both pass. Neither looks at the prompt, and the defect is only in the prompt. A change that is correct in the dispatcher and wrong in the text it composes will pass every test written against the dispatcher.

A REVIEW THAT RAN NINETY-TWO MINUTES AND PRODUCED NO REVIEW, FOR TWO REASONS THAT WERE BOTH THE COORDINATOR'S. Recorded because one of them was predicted in this session and then walked into anyway, and the other is a requirement nothing states.

First: an implement-role review receives the landing contract, and does landing work. While the read-only roles were undispatchable, reviews were dispatched at implement to obtain a writable tier. That workaround was flagged at the time with its own hazard — an implement-role review node also receives the landing grant, so it can author a plan comment claiming a landing; a review is not a landing — and the hazard was reported to a peer as something to watch for at merge. It then happened here. The node's own words near the end of its run: let me view the exact insertion points in my tree — end of §20 in the plan, and end of the evidence file. It was composing a landing record instead of its review record, because the prompt it was handed told it to. Predicting a failure mode does not prevent it; only removing the condition does, which is what the role repair did.

Second, and not previously written down anywhere: a review node's worktree must contain the commits it is reviewing. Its own report: my tree lacks the reviewed commits (they're the subject of this review). The node was dispatched while the diff was still unmerged, so its worktree was cut from a base that predates the work it was asked to judge. A reviewer with no access to its subject cannot refuse usefully — it has nothing to read — and this one spent its budget on the only writable thing in front of it. The requirement is a scheduling one: a review is dispatched after its subject is merged, or it is dispatched with the commit reachable in its tree. All six commits under review here were merged before the three replacements went out, and those three are running normally.

The cost, stated plainly: ninety-two minutes of a contended lane, no review record, and three verified landings held in scoring that could not promote. The replacement reviews went to the metered lane instead, which had 79% of its weekly window remaining against a local lane at twenty-plus concurrent — the first routing decision in this session taken from the figures rather than by default, and the one the load measures in §22 exist to make ordinary.

A delivered review enters scoring itself, so the lifecycle prescribes reviewing the review. rev-promotion-dedup read a landed diff, wrote its score to the review store, and went terminal with a manifest — which is the entry condition for scoring. The unreconciled-runs refusal then handed back, as its prescribed disposition, a crew dispatch --role review --node review-of-rev-promotion-dedup. Obeying it would produce a score of a score, whose delivery would enter scoring in turn.

The lifecycle in the table above reads terminal with manifest → scoring → review attached → promotable and does not distinguish the role that produced the terminal run. A review node satisfies every clause of it.

It is bounded in practice only because a coordinator notices and stops. That is the same shape as every other finding here: the rule is right, nothing checks the case it does not cover, and the protection is a person reading the prescription before running it. The condition to add is narrow — a run whose role is review has no review dimension to score, so its terminal disposition is reconciliation, not a further review.

Disposed by discarding the pointer rather than dispatching: the review it produced is on disk and was used to promote promotion-stops-authoring-the-record-the-worker-writes, so the run's evidence is intact and the pointer was the only thing outstanding.

A review that found no defects is indistinguishable from a review that never happened, and the node it cleared sits in scoring while the surface asks for a review that already exists.

the-endpoint-finding-silences-only-a-leaf has a stored review: status: parsed, all five dimensions scored, total 95. Its node stayed scoring, and its next_action read dispatch a review. The gate is recovery.py:196:

and not review.get("absent")

and that record's absent field holds ['no defect found in the fix; the only notes are below in the justifications, none blocking']. A reviewer reporting that it found nothing wrong populated the field whose truthiness means this review does not count.

The field is derived, and also accepted from the record. review.py:161 computes it as [dim for dim in REVIEW_DIMENSIONS if dim not in scores] — the dimensions carrying no recognised SCORE line — and the prompt describes it that way. But review.py:283 reads absent back out of the record and coerces each entry to a string, so an emitted value survives verbatim and overrides the computation. A field that is authored where it should only be calculated is the defect; the naming is what makes a reviewer author it, because "absent" reads as a place to say what was not found.

This is §21's own stated failure mode occurring to §21. The section requires that an unparsed review must not be stored as an absent one, for the same reason a stale hold and an honest unknown must stay distinct. What happened is the third case neither of us named: a fully parsed, high-scoring review stored as an absent one, and the distinction the section exists to protect collapsed from the other direction.

The cost is a node held out of promotion with no signal that anything is wrong — the review is on disk, readable, and scored, and every surface reports it missing. Repair: compute absent and never read it from the record, which also removes the naming trap.

Correction to the comment above: the absent defect misdirects a coordinator, it does not strand a node. I overstated the cost.

I wrote that a node is held out of promotion with no signal that anything is wrong. It is not held. _review_is_complete has exactly one caller, recovery.py:1325, which sets the displayed classification; promotion.py contains no review gate of any kind. A coordinator who simply runs crew complete succeeds. Verified here by grep over the package after a peer reported it.

The peer also measured the frequency, which I had not. Scanning all 33 stored review records for the signature — a non-empty absent beside a non-null total, a pair the computing path cannot produce because review.py:164 sets total = None whenever the computed absent is non-empty — returns 3 of 33, 9%. All three absent values are reviewer prose, which confirms the field name invites the authoring. Two of the three are from 2026-09-14 and both promoted anyway; the third is the one here, still in flight.

So the accurate cost: the surface reports scoring with next_action: dispatch a review for a review already on disk, and a coordinator who trusts the display spends a worker re-reviewing something that was never missing. Misdirection rather than a hold, and it has stranded nobody's work.

Worth keeping the reason the narrower claim reached me at all: the peer's first ledger parse returned zero rows and would have reported both 09-14 runs as unpromoted — "two nodes stranded since yesterday", false. A positive control against a known-promoted run caught it before the claim was sent. That is the same instrument discipline that has corrected four claims on this plan today, applied by its author before publication rather than by a reader afterwards.

s21-score-reader-decomposition — delivered report

Cited from /home/ITER/mcintos/.config/reckon/crew/reports/reckon/s22-coord/s21-score-reader-decomposition/report.md.

# §21 — the review is scored, stored in three durable places, and read by nothing

Decomposition of `docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html` §21 into dispatchable
single-deliverable nodes, against the code as it stands at
`f90aa56ac7708f34e34385bc9e08f99b5a954b27` (worktree
`/home/ITER/mcintos/Code/.reckon-worktrees/reckon-c8f839407e49/s22-coord/s21-score-reader-decomposition`,
`git status --porcelain` empty, so the tree equals the committed blob).

Every citation below is `path:line` read from the committed blob at HEAD via
`git grep … HEAD` or `git show HEAD:<path>`, not from memory and not from the
documentation. One claim — the review store's write exclusivity — was additionally
executed; nothing else here ran code.

**This is a report. No repository file was changed.**

## Verdicts

| # | §21 measure | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| M1 | A score has a reader | **partial** |
| M2 | A dimension below its floor is not averaged away | **landed** |
| M3 | The row it produces requires a disposition | **partial** |
| M4 | The rubric defines each dimension per role | **not-started** |
| M5 | Each dimension names the actor who owns it | **not-started** |
| M6 | The dimensions reach the committed ledger row | **landed** |
| M7 | A score is queryable against the job that earned it and the work it generated | **partial** |
| M8 | Two runs never hold one review record, and the check that says so covers the store | **landed** |

Instrument note, because every "no caller" verdict below rests on a grep: the
same grep finds callers where they exist (`git grep -c 'ledger_block' HEAD --
reckon/crew/promotion.py` → 2 hits at `:4026` and `:4032`) and finds exactly one
line for `review_scores` (`git grep -n 'review_scores' HEAD -- reckon/` → only
the definition), so the absence is a property of the code and not of the search.

---

## M1 — A score has a reader — **partial**

Landed: a stored dimension drives an observable outcome on one path. The
coordinator-obligations view derives one duty per undisposed sub-floor dimension
(`reckon/crew/obligations.py:270` `_sub_floor_items`, called at `:375`), reading
`record["scores"]` through `reckon/crew/review.py:1251` `sub_floor_dimensions`
(`scores` read at `:1268`). That view is pushed at the coordinator every turn
through the hook (`reckon/hooks/coordinator_obligations.py:476`) and is readable
as an MCP crew view (`reckon/mcp.py:3888`). A change of stored score across the
floor changes that output, asserted at `tests/test_sub_floor_dimension_is_an_obligation.py`.

Not landed: no surface reads a score at or above its floor, and the queryable
reader built for this section has no caller. `reckon/ledger.py:2364` defines
`review_scores(records, *, plan, node, run_id)`; `git grep -n 'review_scores'
HEAD -- reckon/` returns only that definition line — its only callers are tests
(`tests/test_ledger.py:876/906/926`). The other production read of a stored
review is a completeness check, not a reader of scores:
`reckon/crew/recovery.py:576` reads `review.get("scores")` to ask whether all
five dimensions are present.

So the measure's strict evidence — "a change to a stored score changes an
observable outcome" — holds only for a score below its floor. A durability of 12
against a floor of 10, or any above-floor score, changes nothing anywhere.
This is the "act on the scores" half of the lead's 2026-09-14 directive and it
is the reason nodes N1 and N5 below exist.

## M2 — A dimension below its floor is not averaged away — **landed**

- Floor declared in flight config beside the other gate settings, per dimension:
  `reckon/crew/review.py:1210` `declared_dimension_floors` reads
  `gates.dimension_floors`; shipped default `reckon/schema/flight-defaults.yaml:109`
  (all five dimensions at 10, half the 0..20 scale, with the reasoning in the
  comment above it); schema source `reckon/schema/flight.yaml:707`; generated
  artefacts `reckon/_flight_schema.py:425` and `docs/_shared/flight.schema.json:1002`.
- The total is never consulted: `reckon/crew/review.py:1251` returns a row per
  scored dimension below its floor, and the obligations rows are derived from
  that list alone (`reckon/crew/obligations.py:329`).
- The row exists as evidence a reader sees: `reckon/crew/obligations.py:44`
  `SUB_FLOOR_DUTY_KIND = "review-dimension-sub-floor"`, naming run, dimension,
  score and floor (`reckon/crew/obligations.py:322-333`).
- Selection is revision-aware, so a superseded record cannot stand in:
  `reckon/crew/obligations.py:303` uses `recovery.select_review_for_head`.
- Test: `tests/test_sub_floor_dimension_is_an_obligation.py` (the section's
  2026-09-28 landing record, `docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:3240`,
  reports 6 failed at base → 7 passed at head).

Honest caveat carried from the section's own followup
(`docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:1971-1975`): "no test fails if the shipped
default floors are removed", so the shipped default in `flight-defaults.yaml` is
not itself pinned. That is a test-coverage gap on a landed measure, not an
unlanded measure; it travels with N2.

## M3 — The row it produces requires a disposition — **partial**

Landed: the closed set, its validity rule, the retiral semantics and the writer
function all exist.

- Closed set: `reckon/crew/review.py:1188`
  `DIMENSION_DISPOSITION_KINDS = ("folded", "exempted")`, stored per dimension
  under `reckon/crew/review.py:1181` `dimension_dispositions`.
- Validity: `reckon/crew/review.py:1234` `dimension_disposition_valid` — a fold
  must name a node id, an exemption must carry a reason; anything else leaves the
  row standing.
- A row retires only through a valid disposition of the closed set:
  `reckon/crew/review.py:1271-1287`.
- Writer: `reckon/crew/review.py:1289` `record_dimension_disposition`.

Not landed, in two distinct halves, and they are two different deliverables:

1. **Nothing in production writes a disposition.** `git grep -n
   'record_dimension_disposition' HEAD` returns the definition and six test call
   sites (`tests/test_sub_floor_dimension_is_an_obligation.py:267/287/291/295/325/349`)
   and no production caller. A coordinator whose obligations view names a
   sub-floor dimension has no command that disposes of it; the only moves are
   hand-editing the store or promoting the run, which removes the live pointer
   the row reads. The instruction the row itself carries is already written —
   "dispose <dimension> scored <n> against a floor of <n> on run <id>: folded
   with the dispatched node's id, or exempted with the recorded reason"
   (`reckon/crew/obligations.py:326-331`) — so the surface names a disposal the
   system cannot yet perform. This is already recorded as the open followup
   `f-cot-sub-floor-disposition-has-a-writer`
   (`docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:1971-1975`).
2. **The session-closure reading does not count the row.** The measure's stated
   assertion is "requiring the drain ledger's foldable-remaining to count an
   undisposed sub-floor dimension, so a session cannot report a clean close over
   one". `reckon/crew/runs.py:993` `drain` derives entirely from live pointers
   (`unreconciled_runs` at `:1043`, `executable_remainder` at `:1044`, `drained`
   at `:1046`) and consults no review state; the term "foldable" does not occur
   anywhere in `reckon/` (`git grep -ni 'foldable' HEAD -- reckon/` → nothing),
   so there is no foldable-remaining figure to count with. What exists is the
   obligations `summary.count` (`reckon/crew/obligations.py:392-397`), which does
   include the rows, but that is a different surface from the closure reading the
   measure names.

## M4 — The rubric defines each dimension per role — **not-started**

The node-review rubric has one definition of durability, applied to every role.
`reckon/crew/prompts/review.md:78` — "durability — a test exists that fails if
this change regresses" — and nothing in the file or in the code branches on
role: the dimension list at `reckon/crew/prompts/review.md:73-80` is
unconditional, and the schema names the five dimensions once
(`reckon/crew/review.py:73` `REVIEW_DIMENSIONS`).

Two facts about how that text reaches a reviewer, both of which shape N4:

- `reckon/crew/review.py:224` `load_review_prompt` reads the file, and its only
  callers are tests (`tests/test_review_prompt_contract.py:64/74`,
  `tests/test_review_scoring.py:79/105/107`) — `git grep -n 'load_review_prompt'
  HEAD -- '*.py'` returns no production call site.
- The composed worker prompt carries no rubric text and no pointer to that file:
  `reckon/crew/prompts.py:257` `compose_prompt` builds it from the fences and the
  node's own goal, done-when and write paths. Checked against a live review run
  on this host — `r-20260928T180707688785-review-of-preflight-reports-runs-remaining`,
  whose 129-line `prompt.txt` names neither "dimension" nor `review.md` — while
  the record that run wrote does carry all five dimension names
  (`~/.config/reckon/crew/reviews/reckon/r-20260928T140618988787-preflight-reports-runs-remaining.json`,
  `scores` = goal_fidelity/evidence/scope_discipline/durability/fit). So the
  rubric reaches reviewers by a route this reading did not establish — the plan
  names the five dimensions in prose (`docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:1863`),
  and a coordinator may name the file in a goal — and **N4 must establish that
  route before editing the rubric text**, because a per-role definition written
  into a file nothing loads changes no reviewer's behaviour.

The document-shaped deliverable is real and gated on a review —
`reckon/crew/promotion.py:2928` reads "a documentation node writing docs and an
investigate node writing a report" as work a reviewer must read — so a document
node is scored on the code definition of durability and can only score low on it
for the reason the section gave: no regression test can exist for a document.

Separate mechanisms exist and must not be mistaken for this measure. The plan
review store has its own item sets — `reckon/crew/plan_review.py:105`
`PLAN_REVIEW_RUBRICS = ("plan_review", "plan_design_review")`, prompts at
`reckon/crew/prompts/plan_review.md` and `plan_design_review.md` — but those are a
different rubric over a *plan* (`PLAN_REVIEW_ITEMS` at
`reckon/crew/review.py:108`, `PLAN_DESIGN_REVIEW_ITEMS` at `:117`), scored on
whether a finding "would have changed the plan"
(`reckon/crew/review.py:102-107`), not the five-dimension node rubric applied with
a per-role definition. The measure asks for the same rubric to define a dimension
differently per role so that a versioned, asserted-over document can reach a high
durability score at all; nothing implements that.

## M5 — Each dimension names the actor who owns it — **not-started**

No ownership concept exists. The parsed record shape carries status, scores,
absent, justifications, item verdicts, findings, total and raw text
(`reckon/crew/review.py:398-420`) and no per-dimension actor field; the ledger
block carries status/scores/absent/total only (`reckon/crew/review.py:1124-1155`).
`git grep -niE 'owning_actor|attributable|brief_owned|coordinator_owned|worker_owned|owned_by' HEAD -- reckon/`
returns nothing. The rubric prompt likewise never asks a reviewer whether a low
score is attributable to the worker's conduct or to the brief, fence or write
path the coordinator set — the distinction the section's own analysis makes
(the two measured durability-5 cases are coordinator-owned, the scope discipline
is worker-owned). The routing half of the measure (a repair from a sub-floor
dimension reaching the owning actor) therefore has nothing to route on.

## M6 — The dimensions reach the committed ledger row — **landed**

- The compact block is built by `reckon/crew/review.py:1124` `ledger_block` and
  written at promotion: `reckon/crew/promotion.py:4026` and `:4032` (the
  `unreadable` case and the stored case).
- Measured at HEAD over the committed ledger: 173 of 461 rows in
  `docs/state/reckon/runs/*.json` carry a non-null `review` block, each with the
  key set `(absent, scores, status, total)` — against the section's stated 0 of
  854 at writing (`docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:1544`). (Counted with
  a JSON scan of the committed files in this worktree; a positive control on the
  same scan is that the key set is exactly the one `ledger_block` emits.)
- The negative half — an absent review must not read like a scored zero — is
  implemented in the block's own contract (`reckon/crew/review.py:1127-1133`: an
  unreviewed row stores `None`, and a record that produced no scores keeps a
  status other than `parsed`) and asserted in tests
  (`tests/test_review_scoring.py:379-390`, `tests/test_crew_scoring_state.py:139-171`).

## M7 — A score is queryable against the job that earned it and the work it generated — **partial**

Landed: the query function. `reckon/ledger.py:2364` `review_scores(records, *,
plan, node, run_id)` filters on the row's own run attributes and returns
per-dimension scores from rows carrying a review, with an absent review omitted
rather than zeroed (documented in its docstring, `reckon/ledger.py:2371-2380`).
Tested at `tests/test_ledger.py:876`.

Not landed, two things:

1. **No production caller** — as under M1: `git grep -n 'review_scores' HEAD --
   reckon/` returns one line, the definition. The joiner exists and nothing joins.
2. **The join stops at the parent run.** The measure asks for dimensions to join
   "onward to the rows that run produced", so that "which dimension was low on the
   jobs that later generated repair work" is answerable from committed state. The
   returned rows carry `run_id`, `plan`, `node`, `status`, `scores`, `absent` and
   `total` (`reckon/ledger.py:2396-2405`) and nothing that names work the run
   generated. No key for that exists in the ledger row: the row has no
   forward-link to the obligations rows or followups a run spawned.

## M8 — Two runs never hold one review record, and the check that says so covers the store — **landed**

Enforced and executed here, not merely read.

- A review node's declared write paths are the store paths under the crew config
  home, outside every repository: `reckon/crew/recovery.py:420-424` composes the
  legacy path and the head-keyed path via `review_path`
  (`reckon/crew/review.py:760`).
- Out-of-repository declared paths are not dropped by the scope resolver: they
  resolve to a `None` repository and are carried as absolute paths
  (`reckon/crew/dispatch.py:1076-1081`), and the refusal matches them by component
  overlap rather than by repository membership
  (`reckon/crew/dispatch.py:1552` `_raise_repository_scope_conflict`; the
  repository guard at `:1576-1578` compares `None` to `None` for two store paths
  and therefore does *not* skip them).
- Assertion, executed at HEAD: `PYTHONPATH=$PWD
  /home/ITER/mcintos/Code/reckon/.venv/bin/python -m pytest -p no:cacheprovider -q
  tests/test_scope_refusal_names_its_claimant.py` → **3 passed in 8.80s**. The
  positive case publishes a live pointer holding both review-store paths and
  requires the second dispatch to be refused with exit 7, `error ==
  "scope-conflict"` and `conflicting_run_id == CLAIMANT_RUN`
  (`tests/test_scope_refusal_names_its_claimant.py:228-249`); the negative
  control is the same call with no claimant, which dispatches normally
  (`:272-302`).

Residual, reported rather than proposed as a node because the measure's assertion
passes: a *claim-versus-claim* collision is still not surfaced as a conflict.
The scopes view groups claims by path, so two live runs appear under one key
(`reckon/mcp.py:3942-3951`), while `live_conflicts` compares candidate nodes
against live claims only (`reckon/crew/runs.py:757-770`), which is exactly the
shape the section measured on 2026-09-14. Enforcement fires at dispatch; the
read-only view that would have shown it in advance still does not flag it, and
the measure's second negative ("two runs reviewing *different* subjects are
admitted") is covered only indirectly, by the no-claimant control.

## Node proposals

Five nodes, one per unlanded measure half. Ids are proposed names for the lead;
each goal names **one** deliverable. "Fails at base" is stated as the observable
that must be red at the current HEAD before the node starts.

### N1 — `a-score-is-queryable-from-committed-state`

- **Goal:** per-dimension scores are readable against the job that earned them
  from committed state through a production surface, instead of only from an
  uncalled library function.
- **Done-when:** a test that invokes the production surface (a `crew` MCP view or
  a `reckon ledger` subcommand — see decision 6) over a fixture ledger with a
  reviewed and an unreviewed row asserts the reviewed row's five dimensions come
  back filtered by plan / node / run_id and the unreviewed row is absent.
  **Fails at base:** the surface has no such view/verb, and `review_scores` has
  no caller, so the call fails rather than returning the wrong rows.
- **Write paths (exclusive):** `reckon/ledger.py`, plus exactly one surface file
  (`reckon/mcp.py` **or** `reckon/cli.py`), plus
  `tests/test_review_scores_are_queryable.py`.
- **Negative control:** the same fixture with the review block removed from the
  reviewed row must return empty, not a row of zeros; and querying a run whose
  stored review is `unparsed` must return its status without inventing scores.
  Mutation to prove the guard: drop the `isinstance(block, Mapping)` guard in
  `reckon/ledger.py:2392` and the absence case must redden.
- **Order:** first — N5 and N7-repair selection would read scores through it.

### N2 — `a-sub-floor-disposition-is-written-by-a-command`

- **Goal:** the closed disposition set gets a command-line writer, so a
  coordinator retires a sub-floor obligation without editing the store by hand.
- **Done-when:** a test that runs the command for both kinds — `folded` with a
  node id, `exempted` with a reason — and asserts the obligations row disappears
  on the next read, while an unknown dimension, an unknown kind, a fold with no
  node and an exemption with no reason are each refused and leave the row
  standing. **Fails at base:** no command writes a `dimension_dispositions`
  entry (`record_dimension_disposition` is called only from tests), so the row
  survives every invocation.
- **Write paths (exclusive):** `reckon/cli.py`, `reckon/crew/review.py`,
  `tests/test_sub_floor_disposition_has_a_writer.py`.
- **Negative control:** the refusal case above is the red log — the declared
  mutation removes `dimension_disposition_valid`'s kind check and the
  "unknown kind is refused" assertion fails on the log's first line. Carry the
  two smaller findings from `docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:1971-1975` into
  this node's done-when: the comment at `reckon/crew/review.py:1166`
  ("a floor of zero would report every dimension of every review") is wrong — a
  floor of 0 reports *nothing* because every score is ≥ 0 — and a test must fail
  if the shipped default floors in `reckon/schema/flight-defaults.yaml:109` are
  removed.
- **Order:** independent of N1; ahead of N5's routing half, which needs a
  disposition to exist before routing can be observed. This node is what the open
  followup `f-cot-sub-floor-disposition-has-a-writer` already asks for; dispatch
  it against that followup rather than minting a second one.

### N3 — `a-clean-close-counts-an-undisposed-sub-floor-row`

- **Goal:** the closure reading a coordinator consults counts an undisposed
  sub-floor dimension, so a session cannot report a clean close over one.
- **Done-when:** a test builds a session whose only outstanding item is an
  undisposed sub-floor dimension and asserts the closure figure counts it (and
  that a disposed row, and a clean review, do not); **fails at base**, where the
  closure reading (`reckon/crew/runs.py:993` `drain`, `unreconciled_runs` at
  `:1043`) has no review term at all.
- **Write paths (exclusive):** `reckon/crew/runs.py`, `reckon/crew/obligations.py`,
  `tests/test_closure_counts_a_sub_floor_row.py`.
- **Negative control:** dispose the row through `record_dimension_disposition`
  and the count must drop to zero; mutation: make `sub_floor_dimensions` ignore
  dispositions and the disposed-case assertion reddens. A second negative: a
  run whose review is entirely above its floors contributes zero.
- **Order:** after N2 (the disposal path must exist to assert the retiral) and
  after decision 3 is settled (see below), because the target surface is the
  lead's choice.

### N4 — `the-rubric-defines-each-dimension-per-role`

- **Goal:** the node review rubric applies a per-role definition of each
  dimension, so a document deliverable is scored against "the record is versioned
  and something reads it" rather than "a test fails if this regresses".
- **Done-when:** a test scoring one document-role node and one code node against
  the same rubric requires the definition applied to differ, and the negative
  half requires a version-controlled, asserted-over document to be able to reach
  a high durability score. **Fails at base:** the rubric carries a single
  durability definition (`reckon/crew/prompts/review.md:78`) with no role branch,
  so a document node's durability sentence is byte-identical to a code node's.
  Two readings this node must make first, both cheap and both able to move the
  fix: (a) establish the route by which the rubric reaches a reviewer, since
  `load_review_prompt` has no production caller and `compose_prompt` carries no
  rubric text — if the reached text is not the file, editing the file changes
  nothing; (b) decide whether the definition should key on the node's *role* or
  on its *deliverable* (decision 4 below), because a role that writes both a
  document and a test cannot be served by either alone.
- **Write paths (exclusive):** `reckon/crew/prompts/review.md`,
  `reckon/crew/review.py`, `reckon/crew/prompts.py` if (a) shows the composer is
  where the rubric must travel, `tests/test_the_rubric_is_per_role.py`.
- **Negative control:** the guard must be the mirror falsifier that already holds
  the prompt to the schema (the dimension-name mirror noted at
  `reckon/crew/review.py:70-76`) extended to the role split: remove the role
  branch and the "definitions differ" assertion must redden. A second negative:
  an unknown role must fall back to the code definition rather than to none. A
  third, aimed at (a): the assertion must fail if the rubric text stops reaching
  the reviewer at all, which is the failure a prompt-file-only edit produces.
- **Order:** independent; serialize against N2/N5 on `reckon/crew/review.py`.

### N5 — `each-dimension-names-its-owning-actor`

- **Goal:** each dimension's record states whether the score is attributable to
  the worker's conduct or to the brief, fence or write path the coordinator set,
  and a sub-floor finding is routed to that actor.
- **Done-when:** a test parses a review whose durability is coordinator-owned and
  whose scope discipline is worker-owned and asserts the record carries the
  per-dimension actor, plus a routing case: a coordinator-owned below-floor
  dimension lands in the coordinator's own queue, a worker-owned one names the
  roster member. **Fails at base:** the parsed record has no actor field
  (`reckon/crew/review.py:398-420`) and the rubric never asks the question
  (`reckon/crew/prompts/review.md:66-80`).
- **Write paths (exclusive):** `reckon/crew/prompts/review.md`,
  `reckon/crew/review.py`, `reckon/crew/obligations.py`,
  `tests/test_a_dimension_names_its_owner.py`.
- **Negative control:** an unrecognised actor value must be treated as
  unattributed — the row stands and names no owner — never silently defaulted to
  the worker; mutation: default the missing actor to `worker` and the
  unattributed-case assertion must redden.
- **Order:** last of the review-module chain (after N2 and N4, both of which
  write `reckon/crew/review.py` and the rubric prompt); its routing half also
  benefits from N1's reader.

### Overlap ledger

- `reckon/crew/review.py` — N2, N4, N5: one serial chain.
- `reckon/crew/obligations.py` — N3, N5: serialize.
- `reckon/cli.py` — N2 (and N1 if the CLI is chosen): the s22-currency report
  already records `reckon/cli.py` as claimed by another proposal, so N1 should
  prefer the MCP view to avoid it.
- `reckon/ledger.py` — N1 alone.
- `reckon/crew/runs.py` — N3; the same file is in the s14/s19/s21 chain named by
  the currency report, so sequence it there.

## Open design decisions for the lead

1. **Per-dimension floor values.** Landed default: all five at 10 (half the 0..20
   scale) in `reckon/schema/flight-defaults.yaml:109`, overridable at host or
   project layer. Options: (a) keep the uniform half-scale floor; (b) differentiate
   — e.g. a higher durability floor, since the section's measured failure is a
   durability of 5; (c) floor only the dimensions whose low score implies
   follow-up work and leave the rest floorless. The plan settles none of these;
   note that a floor of 0 is a no-op (`reckon/crew/review.py:1166` misdescribes
   this), so "no floor" and "floor 0" are the same state and should not both be
   expressible.
2. **The closed disposition set's representation.** Landed shape: a
   `dimension_dispositions` mapping on the stored record, keyed by dimension
   name, each entry `{kind: folded|exempted, node|reason}`
   (`reckon/crew/review.py:1181-1188`). Open: (a) whether an exemption must also
   record the "authority, dissent, owner or context figure" the measure's text
   names, or a bare reason suffices (today a bare non-empty reason is valid,
   `reckon/crew/review.py:1243-1247`); (b) whether a disposition is keyed to the
   head-keyed record it answers or to the run (today the writer rewrites the path
   it read from, so a re-review at a new head starts undisposed); (c) who may
   write it — any session, the reviewed run's session, or only a coordinator —
   which is the same question `closure_disposition` already answers for pointers.
3. **Where an undisposed sub-floor row counts for closure.** The measure names the
   drain ledger's foldable-remaining; the code has no foldable concept and
   `drain` is pointer-derived only. Options: (a) add a review term to
   `runs.drain` so the closure figure itself counts it; (b) keep `drain`
   pointer-only and have the caller combine it with the obligations summary;
   (c) introduce an explicit foldable-remaining figure as the union of live
   pointer rows and sub-floor rows. (c) matches the plan's language most closely
   and is the largest change.
4. **Where the per-role rubric lives.** Options: (a) one prompt file with a
   role/keyed dimension definition section (smallest diff, keeps the existing
   mirror falsifier); (b) a separate rubric file per deliverable kind, following
   the plan-review precedent (`PLAN_REVIEW_RUBRICS`,
   `reckon/crew/review.py:105`), at the cost that the two rubrics then drift and
   nothing compares them; (c) key the definition on the node's *deliverable*
   (code vs document, readable from the diff's paths) rather than on the role,
   which is what the measure's own wording describes ("a node that changes code"
   vs "a node whose deliverable is a document") and does not depend on a role
   name that a differently-roled node could falsify. The plan leaves this open;
   (c) is the only one that survives a role that writes both.
5. **How the owning actor is recorded and where a repair is routed.** Options:
   (a) the reviewer authors a per-dimension actor field in the review record;
   (b) the reader derives it from the node's authority (write paths, fence,
   brief) — cheaper for the reviewer, but the section's point is that the
   reviewer's own read is the evidence about cause; (c) a hybrid: reviewer
   authors, reader falls back to the brief's shape when absent. Routing target is
   likewise open: a coordinator-owned row could enter the obligations list with
   no `run_id`, or become its own duty kind beside `review-dimension-sub-floor`.
6. **Which surface reads the scores, and what "the work it generated" keys on.**
   Options for the reader: an MCP crew view (`reckon/mcp.py:3865` already lists
   views), a `reckon ledger` subcommand, or the obligations hook. Options for the
   join: join on the reviewed run's node id against the obligation rows that
   carry a `folded` node id, or carry a `generated_node_ids` list on the ledger
   row at promotion. The plan names the join but not its key.
7. **Whether M1's remaining half is in scope at all.** The floor gives a
   below-floor score a reader. The plan's directive is broader — "we need to act
   on the scores" — so the lead should decide whether an above-floor score must
   drive anything (routing, tier selection, promotion weight) or whether the
   floor is the intended and complete reader. If the latter, M1 is landed once
   N1 lands and no node should touch above-floor semantics; if the former, §21
   needs a further measure the table does not currently contain, and this report
   should be read as decomposing only the table as written.

## What this report does not do

It does not verify the merged result of any node, does not edit the plan, and
does not change a repository file. The verdicts above are readings of the
committed blob at HEAD plus one executed test file
(`tests/test_scope_refusal_names_its_claimant.py`, 3 passed).

§22 — The lane's load is measured, pushed at the moment of dispatch, and never a cap

reckon-ship · 2026-09-15T07:05:00Z

THE TOKEN DEFINITION IS CORRECT AND CONSISTENT, AND THIS SECTION'S OWN FIGURE WAS MEASURED ON THE WRONG POPULATION. The lead asked whether tok/s counts thinking. It does, and the empirical test settles it rather than the field names. On one completed run the terminal record reports output_tokens: 26,690, against an emitted-character estimate of 7,327 tokens for text and tool input alone and 24,284 with thinking included. The reported total tracks the second within ten percent, so thinking is inside output_tokens. The sibling detail field output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens reads 0 and means only that this wrapper leaves the breakdown unpopulated — it is not an exclusion, and reading it as one would invert the conclusion.

The per-dialect asymmetry is correct, not a defect. _CODEX_OUTPUT_FIELDS sums output_tokens and reasoning_output_tokens because that dialect reports reasoning separately; _CLAUDE_OUTPUT_FIELDS takes output_tokens alone because that shape already folds thinking in. Both count the same thing. The two field lists look inconsistent and are the only way to be consistent.

Correction to the measure row above. The 1.44 tok/s recorded there is emitted text only — a character proxy this coordinator computed by hand, excluding thinking, which is 73% of emitted characters on the run measured. It understates generation by roughly a factor of four and should not be read as this lane's throughput. The measured figures are below.

The lane is logged, contrary to the premise the section was written under. The committed ledger carries 262 local-lane rows with a rate, spanning 2026-08-26 to today, each with both denominators:

window     n    per-worker median   wall median   NET (sum gen / sum gen-seconds)
all time  262        22.54 tok/s     19.49 tok/s        18.47 tok/s
last 50    50        15.36           15.13              19.74
last 20    20        53.11           50.88              40.34

So the gap is narrower and sharper than stated: the history exists and the live reading does not. Measured on a run in flight, all 190 assistant usage blocks report output_tokens: 0; the true total appears only in the terminal result record. Throughput is therefore not computable for a running worker from the usage stream at all — which is the mechanical reason no live figure exists, and it means this section's live-reading measures cannot be satisfied by aggregating a field that is zero until the run ends. Either the wrapper populates per-block usage, or a live estimate is derived from emitted characters and declared as an estimate, which is this plan's standing rule about a figure naming the population it counted.

And a selection effect that makes the logged history flatter than the truth. The ledger holds only runs that completed. Under contention the slow runs are still running, so recent completions are biased toward the fast ones — which is why the last twenty rows read 53 tok/s per worker while today's live fleet crawls. A lane's logged throughput therefore over-reports exactly when contention is worst, and any routing rule read off the history without that caveat will widen a lane at the moment it should narrow it.

reckon-ship · 2026-09-15T07:20:00Z

THE LIVE TICKER IS THE RIGHT INSTRUMENT, AND THE LANDED HISTORY IS NOT BROKEN — IT IS THE WRONG STATISTIC FOR THROUGHPUT AND THE RIGHT ONE FOR CALIBRATION. Asked by the lead, and the design falls out of three measurements rather than a preference.

First, the engine will not tell us. The locally served endpoint answers /v1/models with 200 and returns 404 on /metrics, /v1/metrics, /status, /health and /stats. There is no Prometheus surface, no running-request gauge, no queue depth. So §17's measure a saturated lane is read from the engine's own counter cannot be satisfied as written on this deployment; the counter does not exist to read.

Second, the protocol will not tell us either. Every assistant usage block on a run in flight reports output_tokens: 0, with the true total appearing only in the terminal result record. So no token-denominated live rate can be derived from the stream's own accounting.

Third, characters are live, and the conversion to tokens is stable. Measured across 72 completed streams carrying a terminal total, emitted characters over reported output tokens:

median 3.65   mean 3.64   stdev 0.19
IQR    3.54 .. 3.74       range 3.14 .. 4.16

A ±5% typical error against a routing question that needs to separate 20 tok/s from 2 tok/s — an order of magnitude — is ample. The estimate is sound; what it must never do is present itself as a measurement.

So the design is a rolling sampler in the follower, which already reads every stream continuously. Per tick, per run: emitted characters since the last tick, over the interval, divided by the calibration factor. Summed per lane it gives net serve throughput; divided by the generating population it gives the per-worker figure; the waiting population is counted separately and excluded from the denominator, which is the distinction that ruled out a cap. No new plumbing — the follower is already a continuous reader of exactly this data.

And the landed history becomes the calibration loop rather than a discarded dataset. It is a survivorship statistic for throughput — only completed runs are in it, so under contention the slow ones are still running and the sample skews fast, which is why its last twenty rows read 53 tok/s while the live fleet crawled. But the chars-per-token ratio does not depend on whether a run was fast, so the same biased dataset is an unbiased estimator of the conversion. Every landing yields a fresh character count and a true token total, re-measuring the factor for free. The dataset that cannot answer how fast is the lane is exactly the one that answers what is a character worth, and wiring the second into the first is what makes the live figure self-correcting instead of a constant somebody has to remember to revisit.

What this changes in the measures above. The live-reading rows stand, with their source named: a sampled estimate from emitted characters, carrying its calibration factor, the sample interval, the generating and waiting counts, and its vintage — never a bare number. The engine-counter row is amended by measurement rather than deleted: it stays the preferred source and is recorded as unavailable on this deployment, so a future serve that does expose counters supersedes the estimate rather than duplicating it.

reckon-ship · 2026-09-15T10:40:00Z

CORRECTION TO THIS SECTION: CONCURRENCY WAS THE SYMPTOM AND THE CAUSE IS A PREFIX-CACHE COLLAPSE. Relayed by a peer coordinator from the serve owner's findings, with an independent measurement of their own. This section recorded that the lane was divided 37 ways and that each additional worker subtracts from every other. The arithmetic is right and the diagnosis it invited is wrong.

Two independent measurements agree, which is what makes the correction trustworthy. This session measured per-worker output by counting emitted characters and converting at the session's own measured thinking share; the peer read the serve's aggregate directly:

this session   37 concurrent   5.41 tok/s per worker   (implied aggregate 200)
peer           36 concurrent   5.50 tok/s per worker   (aggregate 198 measured)
peer           20 concurrent   9.50 tok/s per worker   (aggregate 190 measured)

Aggregate is flat. Dropping the fleet from 36 workers to 20 moved it 198 to 190 tok/s — within noise — where a contention story predicts it roughly holding per-worker and halving total. So shedding workers does not recover throughput; it only redistributes a fixed aggregate, which is why per-worker rate rose while the fleet's output did not. The peer's own instrument says the same from the other side: 13.9 tool calls per ten-minute bucket at ~35 workers against 16.5 at ~19-23, a 19% fleet gain where halving the fleet should have cost half.

The actual constraint. Prefix hit rate measured at 21–25% against an expected ~90%, with 18,863 of 22,557 tok/s of prefill recomputing prefixes the engine had already built. The remedy is a serve restart at a larger KV pool, not a smaller fleet. No amount of dispatch discipline reaches it.

What survives from this section and what does not. The measures stand: a lane that reports no load, a per-row rate with no denominator, and six coordinators each blaming their own node are all real and unchanged. What is withdrawn is the implied remedy — that a coordinator reading a low per-worker figure should dispatch less. It should dispatch less when told the lane is recovering, and otherwise the figure tells it how long a node will take, not that the fleet is at fault. A load reading that invites the wrong remedy is this plan's own subject, so the correction belongs here rather than as a footnote.

A requirement passed with it, and a tension worth naming. The serve owner wants any cap applied at dispatch and never as an admission filter on requests — a request-level refusal killed a worker's compaction and turned a recoverable condition into a dead run reporting a misleading prompt-length error. The figure is derived, (pool_tokens × 0.5) / mean_context_tokens, giving 32 post-restart but 7 at the 167k mean context also seen today, so no constant survives a node-mix change. The tension: the lead has already refused a cap on the grounds that a run parked on a batch job holds a slot and generates nothing, and that objection applies unchanged to a derived cap, because a dispatch cap still counts runs rather than in-flight requests. Recorded as an open conflict between two well-argued positions rather than resolved here; it needs the lead, and it needs the lane document the clive backend does not currently declare.

unknown · undated

The dispatch-time context check admits a request the backend then refuses, because its sum omits its largest term. Two local-lane runs died at 5 s and 6 s with terminal_reason: blocking_limit and one assistant line, Prompt is too long. The refusal is client-side: input_tokens 0, duration_api_ms 0, so nothing was sent. The dry run had reported allowed: true.

routing.py:1506 reads estimated_tokens = standing_tokens + file_tokens — 243,379 repository-file tokens plus a 50,392 standing-instruction floor, 293,771 against a 1,016,576 window. The third term is the member's resumed transcript: both dead runs carried --resume <session-id> for a long-lived roster member, and _context_fit_verdict is handed only resolution and repo, so the omission is structural rather than a missed line.

Three hypotheses were measured and refuted before the cause was found, each sufficient-looking on its own evidence. Plan-file size: refuted — six concurrent runs read the same 765 KB plan successfully. Composed prompt size: refuted — the dead prompts were 12,196 and 13,268 bytes against a working 15,147. Transcript size: refuted, and this is the one worth keeping — resumed transcripts sort orthogonally to the outcome (est. 288 K and 1.08 M tokens died; 692 K, 1.49 M, 2.66 M, 3.03 M and 5.86 M ran clean). The client compacts on resume, so raw transcript bytes do not predict the refusal and must never become the third addend.

That is what makes this the plan's own subject rather than an arithmetic bug. The counted terms are countable and the uncounted one is not — so the honest repair is not a better estimate but an honest verdict: name the resumed session as an input the check does not count, the way headroom: unknown is already, correctly, not read as exhaustion. A sum over two of three terms, reported as allowed: true, is a surface stating a condition it cannot verify.

Operationally the fence is avoidable now: dispatching without --member mints a fresh session. The retry of a-finished-run-is-not-stalled on a session-scoped member has run cleanly for 54 minutes where the roster-member dispatch of the same node died twice.

unknown · undated

One function's deliberately narrow contract is now relied on by five callers, three of which need what it discards — and its docstring still asserts the narrow contract. dispatch.py:3840:

argv = record.get("argv")
if isinstance(argv, list) and argv:
    return {"launch": "cli", "command": argv[0]}

The short-circuit happens before the config lookup, so usable_input_window, model, effort and sandbox are dropped even at call sites that pass a full config. The docstring explains why and is correct about its original purpose: "Only the command matters for reading, and the recorded argv already holds it, so a run stays observable after its config layer changes." True for reading a stream. False for everything else it has since been handed.

Call siteNeeds what is dropped?
promotion.py:1483yes — feeds StreamMeasures, which writes the promoted row's input_utilisation_pct; the divisor is missing, so a row reads 84.2% where the configured window gives 16.6%
dispatch.py:3902 (resume_plan)yes — relaunches on the default model rather than the recorded one
resumption.py:407takes only session_id, so probably unaffected
dispatch.py:3553, 4188reading paths, the original contract

A third consequence, which is this section's own subject. _context_fit_verdict is invoked from exactly one place, routing.py:1601, in the dispatch resolution path. crew resume does not reach it. So a resumed run gets no context check at all — not an honest unknown, not a refusal, simply nothing — and _backend_settings would give it no window to divide by even if it did. Seven runs were resumed in this session under that gap; all succeeded, which is exactly why it stays invisible.

This is distinct from the fit-check finding above and does not replace it. There the check runs and sums two of three terms. Here it does not run.

Found by a peer session working from the utilisation denominator; the resume_plan model consequence was recorded here earlier from the opposite direction. Same line, three consequences, three independent discoveries, none of which found the others. The repair is at the function, not at any caller: a reader that wants only the command can ask for only the command.

§31 — An attempt's exit is never recorded while its worker lives, and a resume refused by a live writer keeps the run working

# S22 plan-currency audit — 17 sections across 3 plans

Base revision of `/home/ITER/mcintos/Code/reckon`: `231e605510ceddee586dfc75560f2ca53dbf70dc` (read with `git log -1 --format=%H` at session start; the worktree base equals main head, `git status --short` clean). Read-only: no repository file was changed by this audit.

Method: for each section, read its own text in the plan HTML under `docs/plans/`, then check code, tests, git log and the committed run records. Every cited sha was verified resolvable with `git cat-file -e`; every cited `file:line` resolves at the base revision. Each plan carries a machine-readable `<meta name="plan-section-declarations">` map (`docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:31`, `docs/plans/a-follower-outlives-its-monitor.html:28`) which is the declaration the executable-remainder and drain fence read; a section's own landing note does not move that declaration (`tests/test_executable_remainder.py::test_landing_evidence_does_not_decrement_the_remainder`).

Vocabulary: **landed-but-undeclared** (done-when holds, declaration still open), **partial**, **not-started**, **superseded**, **blocked**.

---

## crew-observability-truth

Declarations at base: `s1:implementable, s11:done, s12:implementable, s13:deferred, s14–s19:implementable, s20:deferred, s21:implementable, s22:implementable` — 10 implementable. Status `active`, impl 0.45, version 510. **No closure candidate** (8 declared-implementable sections are genuinely open; see below).

### s1 — rationale section — **partial**

The section is a rationale section: it states the five-distinct-ways-the-display-was-wrong finding and names the two defects that were fixed and two that were not. It carries no done-when and no measures, yet the declarations map lists it `implementable`, so it counts toward `plan_executable_remainder` (`reckon/_schema.py:419`) with nothing to implement. That over-count is itself an instance of the defect s14 exists to name (landing evidence is not completion; a declared set must name what is authorable).

- Evidence: `docs/plans/crew-observability-truth.html:31` declares `"s1":"implementable"`; the section body carries no `done when` clause.

**Node `a-measure-less-section-cannot-be-declared-implementable`** — Goal: the declaration grammar refuses `implementable` for a section whose body carries no measure-bearing done-when clause, so the executable remainder counts only sections a worker could actually dispatch. Done-when: `tests/test_executable_remainder.py` gains a case that parses a fixture plan whose section is declared `implementable` but carries no done-when and asserts the read refuses (fails at base where the declaration is accepted; passes after). Reader half landed: `9a2f95e` "fix(crew-reports): refuse a manifest line carrying a second key after its value" and `8417c0f` "fix(crew): the manifest block matches the schema the reader enforces". The guard half is not: `reckon/crew/promotion.py:1319` still swallows a parse refusal — `except (OSError, KeyError, ValueError): return` — so a manifest the reader refuses to parse promotes as a skip, which is exactly the done-when's stated refusal ("proven by feeding it the one-line form and requiring a refusal rather than a skip"). The section's own landing note states this is carried as a follow-on.

- `reckon/crew/promotion.py:1300-1331` `_require_commit_for_changed_manifest`; swallow at :1319; the `CrewError` raise below it is only reachable once the manifest parses.
- Commits `9a2f95e`, `8417c0f` resolve via `git cat-file -e`.

"""Parse the review text and store it to both fenced review-store paths.

Asserts the parse carries all five dimensions in range, then stores the record
and reads it back through the public reader, so the delivered file is proven
to hold what the reader selects. Fenced paths:

  <store>/reckon/<run>.json
  <store>/reckon/<run>.at-9c06bda2abfce2193c465a1d12b53687a05d4fb4.json
"""

import json
import os
import sys
from pathlib import Path

RUN = Path(
    "/home/ITER/mcintos/.config/reckon/crew/runs/"
    "r-20260928T171859933076-review-of-harness-home-lands-in-the-run-directory"
)
REVIEWED = "r-20260928T133831833557-harness-home-lands-in-the-run-directory"
HEAD = "9c06bda2abfce2193c465a1d12b53687a05d4fb4"
BASE = "ff0818f66c00d4d0fe164352f582673358f5fc6a"

os.environ.pop("RECKON_HOME", None)

from reckon.crew.review import (  # noqa: E402
    REVIEW_DIMENSIONS,
    parse_review,
    read_review,
    review_path,
    review_store_root,
    store_review,
)

raw = (RUN / "logs" / "review-raw.txt").read_text(encoding="utf-8")
rec = parse_review(raw)

legacy = review_path("reckon", REVIEWED)
keyed = review_path("reckon", REVIEWED, reviewed_head_sha=HEAD)
print(f"store_root={review_store_root()}")
print(f"legacy_path={legacy}")
print(f"keyed_path={keyed}")
print(f"parse_status={rec['status']} scores={rec['scores']} absent={rec['absent']}")
print(f"total={rec['total']} findings={len(rec['findings'])}")
print(f"items={sorted(rec['item_verdicts'])} absent_items={rec['absent_items']}")
print(f"call_sites={rec['call_site_count']}")

assert rec["status"] == "parsed", rec["status"]
assert sorted(rec["scores"]) == sorted(REVIEW_DIMENSIONS), rec["scores"]
assert all(0 <= v <= 20 for v in rec["scores"].values()), rec["scores"]
assert rec["total"] == 90, rec["total"]
assert not rec["absent_items"], rec["absent_items"]
assert rec["reviewed_base_sha"] == BASE
assert rec["reviewed_head_sha"] == HEAD

record = dict(rec)
record.update(
    {
        "project": "reckon",
        "reviewed_run_id": REVIEWED,
        "review_run_id": (
            "r-20260928T171859933076-review-of-harness-home-lands-in-the-run-directory"
        ),
        "reviewer": "review-of-harness-home-lands-in-the-run-directory",
        "added_failure_count": 0,
        "added_failure_ids": [],
        "added_failures_source": (
            "logs/base-arm-ff0818f6.log and logs/head-arm-9c06bda2.log under "
            "r-20260928T171859933076-review-of-harness-home-lands-in-the-run-directory: "
            "the eleven ids the reviewed run's resume arm reported were run at "
            "ff0818f66c00d4d0fe164352f582673358f5fc6a and "
            "9c06bda2abfce2193c465a1d12b53687a05d4fb4 in git-archive scratch trees "
            "carried on PYTHONPATH, eleven red in each arm with the same ids"
        ),
    }
)

written = store_review(record)
print(f"store_review -> {written}")
assert written == keyed, written
stored_text = written.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
stored = json.loads(stored_text)
assert stored["added_failure_count"] == 0 and stored["added_failure_ids"] == []

tmp = legacy.with_suffix(".json.tmp")
tmp.write_text(stored_text, encoding="utf-8")
tmp.replace(legacy)
print(f"legacy copy bytes={len(stored_text)} == keyed bytes={len(keyed.read_text())}")
assert legacy.read_text(encoding="utf-8") == stored_text

back = read_review("reckon", REVIEWED, reviewed_head_sha=HEAD)
print(
    "read_back="
    f"status={back['status']} total={back['total']} "
    f"added_failure_count={back['added_failure_count']} "
    f"ids={back['added_failure_ids']}"
)
assert back["status"] == "parsed" and back["total"] == 90
assert back["added_failure_count"] == 0 and back["added_failure_ids"] == []
assert len(back["scores"]) == 5
print("STORE OK")
print("EXIT=0")
sys.exit(0)

A live instance of this section's subject arriving from the opposite direction, measured on two runs across two sessions. Both workers correctly had nothing to commit - their write path lies outside every git repository - and both said so in the manifest's commits field in prose. The reader split that prose on commas and returned it as a list of commits. One run's manifest_commits reads ['none - the assigned write path is outside every git repository (git rev-parse --show-toplevel refuses in ~/.config/reckon/crew/reports; its .git entry is an empty directory)', 'so there is nothing to commit to; the durable write is the report file itself'] - two entries, neither a sha, the second a sentence fragment beginning 'so'. The peer's run carries one entry only because its sentence happened to use a semicolon. This section's third measure holds that a terminal phase carrying a PARSED COMMIT beside an unusable status is the cheapest detector; the inverse is now measured, a parsed commit that is prose, and it defeats the same detector by satisfying it. A promotion resolving these against the integration branch would find nothing and record non-reachability for a run that correctly produced no commit, which is a false negative manufactured by the reader rather than reported by the worker. The remedy is this plan's standing rule: a reader that cannot parse a field refuses and names what it expected, rather than returning a shape that type-checks. A commits field whose entries are not commit-shaped is exactly the half-success the second measure forbids.

SECOND RUN REPORTED DEAD WHILE FINISHED, ninety minutes after the first, and it is a DIFFERENT defect - recorded carefully because this coordinator nearly filed it as another run-on before reading the file. The run finished with stop_reason end_turn, subtype success and terminal_reason completed, left a clean worktree, committed 8 files and 427 insertions at 0aa6681, and wrote a 3,973-byte manifest. It classified abandoned, 'the process is gone without a complete manifest'. The manifest is complete. It is written in MARKDOWN HEADING FORM - a '## status' heading with 'complete' beneath it, a '## commits' heading with the sha and subject as a list item, '## changed_paths' with per-file modification markers - and its orientation fields are list items prefixed with a dash rather than bare lines. Every required field is present and correct in substance; not one is in the colon-line syntax the reader requires, so the parse returns status None and commits empty and the classifier reads the absence as a dead worker. THE WORKER DID NOTHING WRONG. It wrote a more readable manifest than the format demands, and nothing in its contract told it the format was strict rather than conventional. This is the second measure of this section - a reader refuses rather than half-succeeds - failing in its purest form: the reader did not raise naming the path and the format it expected, it returned a partial mapping with the two fields that matter missing, which is indistinguishable from a worker that omitted them. TWO INSTANCES, TWO MECHANISMS, ONE VERDICT. The first had the fields present and the value corrupted by a run-on that ate the commits; this has the fields present in the document and absent from the parse. Neither is caught by the two-fields-disagreeing detector, because in one a single defect took both fields and in the other neither field arrived. The remedy proposed against the first instance covers both and should be implemented as the primary rule rather than the fallback: A RUN WHOSE WORKTREE CARRIES COMMITS BEYOND ITS BASE IS NEVER CLASSIFIED ABANDONED, because that fact lives in git and cannot be destroyed by any manifest format. Both runs would have been correctly classified by it without the parser being touched at all.

ROOT CAUSE for a run reported dead while alive, from a peer fleet's monitor pane and measured here. The pane shows one node going working to abandoned at 21:11:04 and abandoned to working at 21:30:27 - the same node, flapping, so the verdict was never true. Two compounding causes, both counted rather than inferred. FIRST, the declared-wait facility exists and nothing reaches it: recovery.py references wait_condition, wait_probe, wait_terminal, wait_started_at and resume_brief across 24 sites, fully built, and the number of manifests that have ever used it across every project and all of time is FIVE, against nineteen parks on one project in one day. A worker submits a detached scheduler job, its process exits, nothing declares the wait, and the classifier says 'the process is gone without a complete manifest' - a true sentence about a live run. SECOND, the non-terminal vocabulary is one word. NON_TERMINAL_MANIFEST_STATUSES is exactly in-progress, while ten live manifests on that project carry five spellings: pending, in-progress, in_progress, running, and one that parses to nothing. Four of five are unrecognised, so the status drops to none and the classifier is left with process liveness alone, which for a parked worker means dead. The two compose: an unusable status plus an undeclared wait leaves nothing but a dead process, and the display reports the only thing it can see. A facility that exists and is never reached is not a facility, which is the rule-with-no-check pattern in a third form - here the rule is reachable, documented, and the template does not make it the path of least resistance.

The sharpest statement of this section's subject, contributed by the lane's owner and arriving from the opposite failure direction to every instance recorded here so far. PROCESS_ALIVE FALSE COVERS FOUR STATES AND NAMES NONE OF THEM: a worker with no live process may have finished, parked deliberately, committed and then died, or genuinely failed. Every reader is left to guess, and both guesses have now been measured. This session's instances are owners failing to wake finished or parked runs. Theirs is the inverse: a coordinator read a node as a casualty - blocked, no live process, dispatched eight hours earlier - and messaged its owner to triage it. The owner corrected them: it had been resumed fourteen times with fourteen commits, was parked on a scheduler job they were actively watching, and the eight-hour stamp was its DISPATCH time rather than when it last worked. No live process is the correct and expected state for a worker that submits a job and ends its turn by design. Same missing field, opposite failures, which is stronger evidence than either alone - it is not a monitoring gap on one side, the state is genuinely unreadable from outside. Their census is worth keeping verbatim in effect: across one day, every run classified abandoned had either committed cleanly or produced nothing, so the classification has never once meant what its name suggests. AND THE DECLARED WAIT MUST BE PROBED, NOT MERELY DECLARED. A field a run asserts and nothing checks is a value nobody can audit after the fact, and would let a run claim it is parked while its job is long gone - the same defect as an admission ceiling that lived only in a launch invocation, or a lane figure published with no observation time. The follower probing the declared job id itself is what turns the declaration into an observation, and it is the load-bearing half rather than the convenient half.

FOUR LINE FORMS DEFEAT THE MANIFEST READER, AND A TERMINAL STREAM EVENT HIDES HOW OFTEN IT HAPPENS. Third spelling reported by a peer coordinator against its own fleet; reproduced here, and a fourth found in the same pass:

status: complete          -> 'complete'      control
- status: complete        -> REFUSED         list prefix
- status: done            -> REFUSED         list prefix (the reported case)
**status:** `complete`    -> REFUSED         emphasis
  status: complete        -> REFUSED         INDENTATION  <- not previously reported
status: done              -> REFUSED         word outside the vocabulary

The accepted vocabulary is blocked, complete, derived, failed, in-progress, in_progress, pending, running, waiting. So done fails on the word and the other four fail on the line shape, which is a different defect wearing the same refusal.

The reader is behaving correctly in every one of these and that is not the problem. It refuses rather than half-succeeding, which is what this section landed. The problem is that it refuses on shapes workers actually emit — a markdown list, a bolded key, an indented block — and a manifest is a document a worker writes by hand under a prose contract, so these are the natural failure modes rather than exotic ones.

The masking is the finding, and it means the observed rate understates the real one. Measured on the peer's run, where every field carries a - prefix:

classification: running      phase: complete
manifest_status: None        manifest_error: None

Three surfaces disagreeing, and the discriminating value is dropped: the reader produced a precise refusal and crew list reports manifest_error: None. The phase reads complete because it comes from the stream's terminal event, so nothing announces that the manifest is unusable. Where the stream carries no terminal event — a worker killed at a ceiling, a process that simply ends — the same run classifies as running forever. So the stream is currently concealing this class, and every count of how often it happens is a lower bound.

This is the second independent sighting of the dropped error. The same manifest_error: None against a precise reader refusal was measured earlier today on this session's own unreadable run. Two sessions, two runs, same silent drop — so it is a property of the surface rather than a quirk of either case.

Two repairs, and the peer is right that the second half is theirs rather than the reader's. Strip list prefixes, emphasis and leading indentation before the split, so the reader is robust to what workers emit; and state the exact plain line form in the worker brief, which the template repair landed this session did for the fields and not for the line shape. Whether done should join the terminal vocabulary is a separate question and is not bundled here.

The reader repair is necessary and is not sufficient: with the manifest readable the classifier would presumably see a terminal status against a dead process and say complete — and presumably is the word that marks an inference nobody measured. The assertion that fences what a coordinator actually sees is a dead process plus a terminal-but-decorated manifest classifies complete rather than stalled, and it cannot be written in the parse-level test file.

Disposition: a sibling node against the classifier, sequenced after the reader lands — not a widening of the node in flight, whose scope is fenced and whose worker is mid-run. Sequenced rather than parallel because the assertion only passes once the parse is fixed, and a test that fails on main to express an intention is a worse artefact than a node that waits.

The observation worth carrying past this instance: three coordinators spent this morning establishing that a starved worker and a stalled one are indistinguishable from outside. A finished one is indistinguishable from stalled too, for an unrelated cause, on the same pane. The pane's stalled verdict is not one defect — it is the place three different conditions arrive wearing the same word.

The rule, stated so it is checkable at authoring: when a reporter supplies the exact string they observed, the done-when carries that string, not a description of its shape. A description is the right form for a property that ranges over a domain; it is the wrong form for a reproduction, because the reproduction is the evidence and paraphrasing it discards the only part that was measured.

And it is the concrete cost of a principle this coordinator stated an hour earlier and did not enforce: that the fix should find the key through decoration generally rather than enumerating known constructs, because the enumeration keeps growing.
