        # will not keep this account's units past logout is a reason to place the
        # watcher outside the manager, and settling this first keeps the seat free
        # for the process that then takes it. Checking after the start would leave
        # a service holding the seat that the fallback could not displace.
        lingering: bool | None = None
        if LINGER_IF_REQUIRED and hasattr(service_manager, "lingering"):
            lingering = bool(service_manager.lingering())
            if not lingering:
                service_manager.enable_linger()
                lingering = bool(service_manager.lingering())
        start_required = bool(changed or restart or not was_active)
        if start_required:
            # 'enable --now' leaves an already-running unit on its old
            # definition, so a rewritten active unit needs an explicit restart.
            service_manager.start(
                project, restart=bool(restart or (changed and was_active))
            )
    except Exception as error:
        from reckon import service

        if isinstance(error, service.LingerUnavailableError):
            return _watcher_armed_as_process(
                project,
                error=error,
                unit_path=path,
                unit_changed=bool(changed),
                environment=environment,
                producer=producer or _arm_watcher_as_process,
                cause=_LINGER_FALLBACK_CAUSE,
            )
        if not _service_manager_unreachable(error):
            raise
        return _watcher_armed_as_process(
            project,
            error=error,
            unit_path=path,
            unit_changed=bool(changed),
            environment=environment,
            producer=producer or _arm_watcher_as_process,
        )

    registration = _register_watch_unit(project, watch_unit_name(project))
    if start_required:
        detail = (
            f"restarted {watch_unit_name(project)} onto a rewritten unit"
            if changed and was_active
            else f"started {watch_unit_name(project)}"
        )
    else:
        detail = (
            f"{watch_unit_name(project)} is already active on an unchanged unit; "
            "started nothing"
        )
    return {
        "project": project,
        "unit": watch_unit_name(project),
        "unit_path": str(path),
        "unit_changed": bool(changed),
        "service_active": was_active or start_required,
        "started": start_required,
        "detail": detail,
        "environment": environment,
        "lingering": lingering,
        "registration": registration,
        "watcher_live": watch_state(project)["watcher_live"],
        # Which path armed the watcher, as a field rather than prose: a caller
        # acts on a value instead of parsing a sentence out of ``detail``.
        "path": "service",
        "fallback_reason": None,
        "ensure_line": watcher_ensure_line(project),
    }


# The two reasons a service arming is abandoned for a plain process. Named
# rather than inlined so the sentence a coordinator reads distinguishes them,
# and so a caller deciding whether a fallback is expected can match on the
# value instead of on a phrase, which drifts.
_SERVICE_UNREACHABLE_CAUSE = "the service manager could not be reached"
_LINGER_FALLBACK_CAUSE = (
    "lingering could not be enabled, so a unit would stop at this account's logout"
)


def _watcher_armed_as_process(
    project: str,
    *,
    error: BaseException,
    unit_path: Path,
    unit_changed: bool,
    environment: Mapping[str, str],
    producer: Callable[[str], Mapping[str, Any]],
    cause: str = _SERVICE_UNREACHABLE_CAUSE,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Arm the watcher as a plain process after the service path was refused.

    The result keeps the shape the service path returns, so a caller reads one
    result either way, and states the fallback in three fields: ``path``, the
    failure that forced it, and whether a watcher is live afterwards. The
    producer reports liveness rather than raising, so a fallback that could not
    start a watcher reads as ``watcher_live`` false with the reason beside it,
    which is the same shape the dispatch path reports.

    ``cause`` names which failure forced the fallback, because two do: a manager
    that cannot be reached, and one that will not keep this account's units past
    logout. The error text alone does not say which, and the sentence a coordinator
    reads has to.
    """
    state = producer(project)
    registration = _register_watch_unit(project, watch_unit_name(project))
    live = bool(state.get("watcher_live"))
    reason = " ".join(str(error).split())
    return {
        "project": project,
        "unit": watch_unit_name(project),
        "unit_path": str(unit_path),
        "unit_changed": bool(unit_changed),
        "service_active": False,
        "started": live,
        "detail": (
            f"{cause} ({reason}); "
            + (
                f"armed the watcher for {project} as a plain background process"
                if live
                else f"a plain background watcher for {project} is not live either"
            )
        ),
        "environment": environment,
        "lingering": None,
        "registration": registration,
        "watcher_live": live,
        "path": "fallback",
        "fallback_reason": reason,
        "ensure_line": watcher_ensure_line(project),
    }


# Every state the watch surface can emit, split by whether a coordinator has to
# act on it. The first set is the vocabulary a reader acts on the sight of; the
# second is progress and is not news on its own. The split used to feed a
# follower state filter, which is gone — a follower now delivers every
# transition — but the vocabulary remains the one the surface knows, and tests
# still assert every emitted state lands in it.
WATCH_ATTENTION_STATES = (
    "complete",
    "blocked",
    "failed",
    "launch-failed",
    "stalled",
    "stopped",
    "abandoned",
    "lane-event",
    "completed_unpromoted",
    "unknown",
    "unreadable",
    "exited-unfinished",
    "wait-aged",
)
WATCH_PROGRESS_STATES = (
    "dispatched",
    "working",
    "running",
    "waiting",
    "promoted",
    "recorded",
)


def _watch_arming_line(project: str) -> str:
    """Return the exact shell-safe command a dispatch payload carries."""
    return f"reckon crew watch --project {shlex.quote(project)}"


# The unit exports this into the watcher's own environment, so the seat record
# a service-armed watcher claims names the unit that will replace it. Read from
# the environment rather than passed as an argument: the watcher's argv is the
# arming contract a person copies, and a path-only flag would appear there.
WATCH_UNIT_ENV = "RECKON_WATCH_UNIT"

# A watcher holds its seat for as long as it runs, so a service that dies at
# logout is the fault this deployment exists to remove: none of the units it
# owns come back, and the project reads as watched until the next dispatch
# refuses. Lingering is what keeps a user manager alive past the last session.
LINGER_IF_REQUIRED = True

# The arming path sets this to the file the watcher it starts must append its
# stdout and stderr to, and the watcher reads it when it takes its seat. Read
# from the environment for the same reason the unit name is: the watcher's argv
# is the arming contract a person copies, and a path-only flag would appear
# there. A watcher a service manager started leaves it unset, because systemd
# already appends the unit's output to that same file.
WATCH_LOG_ENV = "RECKON_WATCH_LOG"

# A watcher's own log is diagnostic, not a ledger, so it is bounded: the file is
# rotated to a single ``.1`` sibling once it passes this size, which keeps the
# most recent output a reader needs to date a producer's death without letting
# an unmanaged watcher fill the shared home over months.
WATCH_LOG_MAX_BYTES = 2 * 1024 * 1024


def ensure_placement_reservation(
    *,
    session: str | None = None,
    project: str | None = None,
    runner: Any | None = None,
    alive_probe: Any | None = None,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Hold the placement reservation if absent, and report it if present.

    The reservation is a durable shared resource of the same kind as the model
    serve and the project watcher, so it is managed the same way: an ensure
    command that is safe to run twice, holding the resource once and reporting
    it afterwards. Its job id is published into the shared crew state rather
    than held in the session that ran the command, because a job id in one
    session's memory is invisible to every other session and each would hold
    its own reservation.
    """
    from reckon.crew import placement as placement_module

    result = placement_module.ensure_reservation(
        session=session, project=project, runner=runner, alive_probe=alive_probe
    )
    result["ensure_line"] = placement_ensure_line()
    return result


def placement_ensure_line() -> str:
    """Return the command that holds or reports the placement reservation."""
    return "reckon crew placement --ensure"


def watch_unit_name(project: str) -> str:
    """Return the systemd user unit that runs one project's watcher service."""
    readable = re.sub(r"[^A-Za-z0-9._-]", "-", project).strip("-") or "project"
    return f"reckon-watch-{readable}.service"


def watch_log_path(project: str) -> Path:
    """Return the file a project's watcher appends its output to.

    One path serves both arming routes, so a reader who finds a dead seat finds
    that producer's last words whichever way it was started: a service manager
    appends the unit's stdout and stderr here, and an unmanaged watcher adopts
    the same file when it takes its seat.
    """
    return _config_home() / "logs" / f"watch-{watch_unit_name(project)}.log"


class _WatchLogStream:
    """A stdout/stderr stand-in that appends timestamped lines to a file.

    A watcher's log is read after the fact, so every line it carries has to say
    when it arrived — otherwise a traceback says what killed the producer but
    not whether that was an hour or a week ago. The file is rotated to a single
    ``.1`` sibling once it passes :data:`WATCH_LOG_MAX_BYTES`, so a watcher left
    running for months cannot fill the shared home.

    Accepts bytes as well as text because a library writing to ``sys.stdout``
    may reach for a binary writer once it sees a non-tty stream, and silently
    dropping those writes would lose exactly the diagnostics this exists for.
    """

    def __init__(self, path: Path, *, max_bytes: int = WATCH_LOG_MAX_BYTES) -> None:
        self.path = Path(path)
        self.max_bytes = max_bytes
        self._handle = None
        # The descriptors this stream owns once it is adopted. They are kept
        # because rotation replaces the file: a descriptor pointed at the log
        # once keeps writing the rotated-away inode, so a library's unbuffered
        # write or the interpreter's own traceback would be lost from the log a
        # reader opens.
        self._descriptors: tuple[int, ...] = ()
        self._at_line_start = True
        self._open()

    def _open(self) -> None:
        self.path.parent.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
        try:
            oversized = self.path.stat().st_size >= self.max_bytes
        except FileNotFoundError:
            oversized = False
        if oversized:
            self.path.replace(self.path.with_name(f"{self.path.name}.1"))
        self._handle = self.path.open("a", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")

    def adopt_descriptors(self, descriptors: Iterable[int]) -> None:
        """Send these process descriptors to this stream's file, and keep them.

        Called by :func:`_adopt_watch_log` once, when the watcher takes its seat.
        Keeping them is what makes the redirection survive rotation: the file a
        descriptor was pointed at is renamed away when the log rotates, so a
        descriptor pointed once and never re-pointed writes an inode nothing
        reads.
        """
        self._descriptors = tuple(descriptors)
        self._point_descriptors()

    def _point_descriptors(self) -> None:
        source = self._handle.fileno()
        for target in self._descriptors:
            try:
                os.dup2(source, target)
            except OSError:
                continue

    def _rotate_if_needed(self) -> None:
        try:
            size = self._handle.tell()
        except (OSError, ValueError):
            return
        if size < self.max_bytes:
            return
        self._handle.close()
        self.path.replace(self.path.with_name(f"{self.path.name}.1"))
        self._handle = self.path.open("a", encoding="utf-8", errors="replace")
        # Re-point every adopted descriptor at the new file. Without this the
        # descriptors keep the rotated-away inode, so a traceback or an
        # unbuffered library write after the first rotation never reaches the
        # log a reader opens.
        self._point_descriptors()

    def write(self, text: Any) -> int:
        if isinstance(text, (bytes, bytearray)):
            text = bytes(text).decode("utf-8", "replace")
        pieces: list[str] = []
        for line in str(text).splitlines(keepends=True):
            if self._at_line_start and line.strip():
                pieces.append(f"[{_utc_now()}] ")
            pieces.append(line)
            self._at_line_start = line.endswith("\n")
        self._rotate_if_needed()
        self._handle.write("".join(pieces))
        self._handle.flush()
        return len(text)

    def flush(self) -> None:
        self._handle.flush()

    def fileno(self) -> int:
        return self._handle.fileno()

    def isatty(self) -> bool:
        return False

    def writable(self) -> bool:
        return True

    def close(self) -> None:
        self._handle.close()


def _adopt_watch_log() -> Path | None:
    """Send this process's stdout and stderr to the log its arming named.

    Called by the watcher when it takes its seat, which is the point at which a
    plain background process becomes the project's producer. Returns the path it
    adopted, or ``None`` when the arming named none — a service-armed watcher's
    output is already appended to that file by its unit, so it has nothing to
    adopt.

    The environment entry is removed on adoption so a watcher that starts
    anything of its own cannot hand the same log on to it. Both the file
    descriptor and the Python streams are redirected: the descriptors so a
    library writing unbuffered output, or the interpreter printing an uncaught
    traceback, still lands in the log, and the Python streams so each line
    carries the time it was written.
    """
    target = os.environ.pop(WATCH_LOG_ENV, "")
    if not target:
        return None
    log = _WatchLogStream(Path(target))
    sys.stdout = log
    sys.stderr = log
    log.adopt_descriptors((1, 2))
    return log.path


def watcher_ensure_line(project: str) -> str:
    """Return the command that starts or restarts a project's watcher service."""
    return f"reckon crew watch --ensure --project {shlex.quote(project)}"


def watch_cycle_line(project: str) -> str:
    """Return the command pair that takes a stale watcher onto current code.

    The ensure command alone cannot do it: a unit already active on an unchanged
    definition is reported rather than restarted, and a watcher armed as a plain
    process is not a unit at all. Releasing the seat first is what makes the
    arming take — ``unwatch`` stops the registered watcher and clears its
    record, so the arming that follows finds no live seat to contend with and
    starts on the code on disk now.
    """
    return (
        f"reckon crew unwatch --project {shlex.quote(project)} && "
        + watcher_ensure_line(project)
    )


def _watch_attach_line(project: str, *, session: str | None = None) -> str:
    """Return the follower one session arms to be woken about its own runs.

    A seat existing is not the same as this session hearing about it: the seat
    is project-global and wake delivery is session-local, so a caller
    dispatching against another session's seat is told a watcher is live while
    nothing reaches it. This is the command that closes that gap.

    The command's first token is the absolute path of the running reckon
    console script, because the shell that arms it need not carry the
    interpreter's bin directory on PATH.

    It is one bare command on purpose: filtering and buffering belong inside
    the follower, because a shell pipeline around it has three ways to swallow
    the ticker silently. An unbuffered stage withholds every line until the
    command exits, and this command does not exit. An unanchored pattern
    matches the summary field that trails each line, so it matches everything.
    And a trailing ``|| true`` turns the follower's own refusal into a silent
    success indistinguishable from a quiet fleet.

    It carries no state filter either. A filter that legitimately matches
    nothing produces an empty pane, which reads the same as a follower that
    never started -- and a reader watching a wave wants the starts and the
    working transitions, not only the landings. A state filter is worse than
    no filter even when it matches: it reports how a run stopped and hides how
    it recovered, which is the half of the story the reader is waiting for.
    """
    parts = [
        shlex.quote(_reckon_console_script()),
        "crew",
        "follow",
        "--project",
        shlex.quote(project),
    ]
    if session:
        parts += ["--session", shlex.quote(session)]
    return " ".join(parts)


def _stream_quiet_seconds(record: Mapping[str, Any], *, now_seconds: float) -> int:
    """Measure quiet time from a stream, with pointer activity as the fallback."""
    stream = Path(str(record.get("log_path") or ""))
    if stream.is_file():
        latest = stream.stat().st_mtime
    else:
        run_id = str(record.get("run_id") or "")
        pointer = pointer_path(run_id) if run_id else Path()
        if run_id and pointer.is_file():
            latest = pointer.stat().st_mtime
        else:
            created = parse_utc(str(record.get("created_at") or ""))
            latest = now_seconds if created is None else created.timestamp()
    return max(0, int(now_seconds - latest))


def _watch_event(project: str, *, stall_seconds: int) -> dict[str, Any] | None:
    from reckon.crew.recovery import _utc_seconds, classify_pointer

    """Return the first terminal or stalled pointer, or the empty-fleet event."""
    pointers = list_live(project=project)
    if not pointers:
        return {
            "project": project,
            "event": "empty",
            "run_id": None,
            "classification": "no_live_pointers",
            "next_action": f"none — project {project!r} has no live pointers",
        }

    moment = _utc_seconds()
    classified = [
        (pointer, classify_pointer(pointer, now_seconds=moment)) for pointer in pointers
    ]
    for pointer, row in classified:
        manifest_status = row.get("manifest_status")
        # A resumed attempt owns evidence newer than the baseline captured at
        # resumption. Completion is never an early placeholder, so the
        # one-event watcher may finish as soon as that attempt writes it even
        # during the short interval before its process exits. Failed and
        # blocked reports remain deferred while the process lives because
        # workers can pre-arm those pessimistic statuses before doing work.
        if (
            manifest_status == "complete"
            or manifest_status in {"blocked", "failed"}
            or (
                pointer.get("attempt_kind") == "resume"
                and row.get("manifest_fresh") is True
                and row.get("manifest_reported_status") == "complete"
            )
        ):
            return {
                "project": project,
                "event": "terminal",
                **row,
                "manifest_status": manifest_status or "complete",
            }

    for pointer, row in classified:
        quiet = _stream_quiet_seconds(pointer, now_seconds=moment)
        if quiet > stall_seconds:
            return {
                "project": project,
                "event": "stalled",
                **row,
                "stalled_for_seconds": quiet,
            }
    return None


def watch(
    project: str,
    *,
    stall_window: str = DEFAULT_WATCH_STALL_WINDOW,
    exit_on_empty: bool = False,
    poll_interval: float = 1.0,
    sleeper: Callable[[float], None] = time.sleep,
) -> dict[str, Any]:
    """Block for a fleet event, optionally treating an empty fleet as a drain."""
    # The single-event arm takes the same seat as the streaming watcher, so it
    # owes the same refusal: a seat held by a watcher that cannot resolve a
    # backend it may be asked to lift reads as armed while it can lift nothing.
    from reckon import flight
    from reckon.crew.dispatch import assert_routable_backends_resolvable

    assert_routable_backends_resolvable(project, flight.resolve(project=project).config)
    stall_seconds = parse_duration(stall_window)
    with _project_watch_claim(project, stall_window) as (acquired, watcher):
        if not acquired:
            return {
                "project": project,
                "event": "watcher-live",
                "run_id": None,
                "classification": "watcher_live",
                "next_action": "wait for the live project watcher to report",
                "watcher_live": True,
                "watcher": watcher,
                "stream_path": str(watch_stream_path(project)),
            }
        while True:
            event = _watch_event(project, stall_seconds=stall_seconds)
            if event is not None and (event["event"] != "empty" or exit_on_empty):
                return event
            sleeper(poll_interval)


def _pointer_claims_worktree(record: Mapping[str, Any]) -> bool:
    """Return whether a pointer must keep its worktree untouched."""
    phase = str(record.get("phase") or "")
    if phase in _TERMINAL_RUN_PHASES:
        return False
    if phase:
        return True
    return record_process_alive(record) is not False


def _live_worktree_claims() -> dict[Path, list[str]]:
    claims: dict[Path, list[str]] = {}
    for record in list_live():
        worktree = record.get("worktree")
        if not worktree or not _pointer_claims_worktree(record):
            continue
        path = Path(str(worktree)).resolve()
        claims.setdefault(path, []).append(str(record.get("run_id") or "unknown"))
    return claims


def process_alive(pid: Any) -> bool | None:
    """Report whether a pid is still running; None when there is no pid.

    A dead process with no terminal event in its log is a recoverable orphan
    rather than a completed run, which is why liveness is recorded beside the
    stream rather than inferred from it. A PermissionError from a zero signal
    means the process exists but belongs to another user — proof of life, not
    death. On a shared workstation carrying several fleets that is the normal
    condition for a peer worker, so reporting it as dead would classify a live
    run as abandoned.
    """
    if not pid:
        return None
    # A zombie is a process-table entry whose process has exited and whose
    # exit status the parent has not yet collected, so the kernel accepts a
    # zero signal against it and the probe below would report the finished
    # run as running: its slot stays held and its own resume is refused while
    # it lingers. Every caller asking whether work is still running wants
    # "no" for a zombie, because the process it was launched to run has
    # finished either way. Reading the state from per-process stat is what
    # tells that apart from the liveness proof above; an unreadable record is
    # not proof of death, so it falls through to the signal probe unchanged.
    if _process_state(pid) == "Z":
        return False
    try:
        os.kill(int(pid), 0)
    except ProcessLookupError:
        return False
    except PermissionError:
        return True
    except (TypeError, ValueError):
        return None
    return True


# The scheduler states that mean a placed job is still in the system: the job
# exists and its work has not ended. Any other readable state means the job has
# left the queue, which is terminal whatever the scheduler calls it. A state the
# scheduler cannot be asked for is None, not False, so a silent scheduler never
# reads as a stopped worker.
_JOB_LIVE_STATES = frozenset(
    {"running", "pending", "configuring", "completing", "suspended"}
)

# A scheduler query is on the liveness path of every read, so it is bounded:
# a controller that hangs must not make a fleet listing hang with it.
_SCHEDULER_QUERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS = 5.0

# The token a query vector carries where the job id is substituted, so a probe
# spells its own argument order rather than reckon guessing one.
_JOB_STATE_PLACEHOLDER = "{job}"


def _scheduler_query_argv(
    placement: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    job_id: Any,
    field: str,
) -> list[str] | None:
    """The argument vector for one field of one job, or None when unknowable.

    The query is read from the placement's own declaration rather than from a
    table keyed on the wrapper's name, so which reporting verb answers a given
    scheduler is configuration. A placement that declares the wrapper without
    declaring how to ask it answers None here and falls through to the pid
    probe, having been refused before launch for exactly that omission.
    """
    if not placement or not job_id:
        return None
    query = placement.get(field)
    if not isinstance(query, Iterable) or isinstance(query, (str, bytes)) or not query:
        return None
    token = str(job_id)
    return [
        token if str(item) == _JOB_STATE_PLACEHOLDER else str(item) for item in query
    ]


def _ask_scheduler(
    argv: list[str] | None, runner: Callable[[list[str]], str | None] | None
) -> str | None:
    """One scheduler question, or None when the question could not be asked.

    The two failures are kept apart because they mean opposite things. A query
    that could not be run — no such scheduler, a non-zero exit, a timeout —
    answers None, and the caller falls back to another instrument. A query that
    ran and printed nothing answers the empty string, which for a job-state
    question is a statement in its own right: the scheduler knows no such job,
    so the job has left the queue. Collapsing the empty answer into None would
    read every ordinary completion as unreadable and send the caller back to a
    pid that belongs to another host.
    """
    if argv is None:
        return None
    probe = _run_scheduler_query if runner is None else runner
    try:
        output = probe(argv)
    except (OSError, subprocess.SubprocessError):
        return None
    if output is None:
        return None
    lines = str(output).strip().splitlines()
    return lines[-1].strip() if lines else ""


def scheduler_job_reason(
    placement: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    job_id: Any,
    runner: Callable[[list[str]], str | None] | None = None,
) -> str | None:
    """The scheduler's own reason string for a placed job, or None.

    A job that never started reports why here rather than through an exit
    status, so a launch-failure record quotes the scheduler's reason instead
    of fabricating one.
    """
    return _ask_scheduler(
        _scheduler_query_argv(placement, job_id, "reason_query"), runner
    )


# A job the scheduler ended for its own reason is not a worker whose work
# failed: the remedy differs, since a resubmission with the same resources fails
# the same way. The two classes a placement plan already names are a time limit
# and a memory limit, matched on the scheduler's own words so a different
# spelling adds a class rather than being read as a failed worker.
_SCHEDULER_KILL_CLASSES: tuple[tuple[frozenset[str], str], ...] = (
    (frozenset({"timeout", "timelimit", "time limit", "deadline"}), "job-timeout"),
    (
        frozenset(
            {
                "out_of_memory",
                "outofmemory",
                "out of memory",
                "oom",
                "memory limit",
            }
        ),
        "job-out-of-memory",
    ),
)


def scheduler_kill_class(state: Any, reason: Any = None) -> str | None:
    """Name the scheduler's own kill reason, or None when it ended for another.

    Matched against both the state and the scheduler's reason string, because a
    scheduler spells a time or memory end in either place and a reason of
    ``None`` is reported differently depending on which one fired.
    """
    haystack = " ".join(part.strip().casefold() for part in (state, reason) if part)
    if not haystack:
        return None
    for spellings, name in _SCHEDULER_KILL_CLASSES:
        if any(spelling in haystack for spelling in spellings):
            return name
    return None


def _run_scheduler_query(argv: list[str]) -> str | None:
    """Run one scheduler state query, answering None when it cannot be read.

    A query that exits non-zero — an unknown job, an unreachable controller —
    answers None rather than an empty string, because the absence of a state is
    not the statement that the job has ended.
    """
    executable = shutil.which(argv[0])
    if executable is None:
        return None
    completed = subprocess.run(
        [executable, *argv[1:]],
        capture_output=True,
        text=True,
        timeout=_SCHEDULER_QUERY_TIMEOUT_SECONDS,
        check=False,
    )
    if completed.returncode != 0:
        return None
    return completed.stdout


def _scheduler_state_argv(
    placement: Mapping[str, Any] | None, job_id: str
) -> list[str] | None:
    """The argument vector that asks a scheduler for one job's state, or None.

    A placement declares the reporting verb that answers one job's state beside
    the wrapper it asks, so a placement that declares no query answers None and
    falls through to the pid probe instead of being read as a stopped job.
    """
    return _scheduler_query_argv(placement, job_id, "state_query")


def scheduler_job_state(
    placement: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    job_id: Any,
    runner: Callable[[list[str]], str | None] | None = None,
) -> str | None:
    """The state a scheduler reports for a placed job, or None when unread.

    Three answers, and the caller must tell the last two apart. A state names
    the job and is read against the in-flight set. The empty string is a
    successful query that named no job: the scheduler knows it not, so it has
    left the queue. None is a question that could not be asked at all — no
    scheduler, no such wrapper, a non-zero exit — and leaves the caller to fall
    back to the pid probe rather than reporting a live run as stopped.
    """
    return _ask_scheduler(_scheduler_state_argv(placement, str(job_id or "")), runner)


def placement_job_alive(
    record: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    runner: Callable[[list[str]], str | None] | None = None,
) -> bool | None:
    """Whether the job a placed run was charged to is still in the system.

    A placed run's recorded pid names the scheduler client, not the worker, so
    the job is the subject of a liveness read. A state the scheduler reports as
    in-flight answers True. Any other readable answer means the job has left the
    queue and answers False, whatever the scheduler calls it — including the
    empty answer of a successful query that named no job, which is how an
    ordinary completion is reported and must not fall through to the pid. A
    record carrying no placement, or one whose scheduler could not be queried at
    all, answers None so the pid probe decides as it always has.

    ``runner`` is the caller's own scheduler query, handed in the way ``alive``
    is so a test reaches this without a scheduler on the host.
    """
    if not record:
        return None
    placement = record.get("placement")
    if not isinstance(placement, Mapping) or not placement:
        return None
    state = scheduler_job_state(placement, record.get("job_id"), runner)
    if state is None:
        return None
    return state.casefold() in _JOB_LIVE_STATES


def record_process_alive(
    record: Mapping[str, Any] | None,
    alive: Callable[[Any], bool | None] | None = None,
    job_alive: Callable[[Mapping[str, Any] | None], bool | None] | None = None,
    match_start_time: bool = True,
) -> bool | None:
    """Report whether the process a run record names is still running.

    Every liveness decision about a run is taken from the run's own record, so
    the pid lookup lives here in one place and the call site never handles a
    bare pid. A record that names no process answers None, the same shape
    :func:`process_alive` already returns for a missing pid, so a caller cannot
    read "no process recorded yet" as a stopped worker.

    A pid the kernel has since handed to another process is not the one the
    record names, and a bare process-table probe cannot tell the two apart: it
    answers liveness for whatever now holds the number. When the record carries
    the kernel start tick written at registration, the probe's answer is kept
    only if the running process is the registered one, so a reused pid stops
    reading as a survivor on every read rather than only where a caller
    remembered to compare. An unreadable start tick is not proof of reuse — the
    same stance :func:`process_alive` takes toward an unreadable process record
    — so the probe's answer stands, which is also what keeps a peer's live
    process readable.

    A placed run is charged to a scheduler job rather than to the coordinator's
    own login slice, so its recorded pid names the scheduler client rather than
    the worker and a local process-table read answers a different question. The
    job is asked first, and the pid probe is the fallback for a record carrying
    no placement or a scheduler that cannot be queried — which keeps an
    unplaced run answering exactly as it always has.

    ``alive`` is the caller's own probe. A module that keeps the primitive
    bound under its own name — so a test can substitute liveness for that
    module — hands it in rather than having its substitution bypassed. The
    reuse check needs the process table, so it is taken only when that real
    primitive answered: a substituted probe is the whole answer for the read.

    ``match_start_time`` is for the one caller that asks whether the process
    itself is running rather than whether it is the registered one. A seat
    guard needs the process that holds the seat, and a running holder is a
    running holder however its recorded identity reads, so it opts out here
    rather than depending on this check being absent.
    """
    if not record:
        return None
    placed = (placement_job_alive if job_alive is None else job_alive)(record)
    if placed is not None:
        return placed
    probe = process_alive if alive is None else alive
    pid = record.get("pid")
    running = probe(pid)
    # The reuse check reads the process table, which is the only thing that can
    # say whether the pid still names the registered process. A caller that
    # substitutes its own probe owns the whole read — its probe answers for
    # liveness and there is nothing left for a second lookup to decide — so the
    # check is skipped when the real primitive is the one that answered. The
    # callers that pass this module's own ``process_alive`` through still get
    # the check on every read they make, and ``alive=None`` resolves to that
    # same function, so the default path is covered by the same identity.
    if running is True and match_start_time and probe is process_alive:
        expected = record.get("pid_start_time")
        if expected is not None:
            actual = _process_start_time(pid)
            if actual is not None:
                running = actual == expected
    return running


def _process_stat_fields(pid: Any) -> list[str]:
    """The space-separated per-process stat fields, or [] when unreadable.

    The comm field is parenthesised and may itself contain spaces and closing
    parentheses, so the split begins after the final ``)``; the fields are the
    third one (state) onwards, unrenumbered from the parenthesised form.
    """
    try:
        value = int(pid)
        stat = Path(f"/proc/{value}/stat").read_text()
    except (OSError, TypeError, ValueError):
        return []
    return stat[stat.rfind(")") + 2 :].split()


def _process_state(pid: Any) -> str | None:
    """The single-character kernel state from the per-process stat record."""
    fields = _process_stat_fields(pid)
    return fields[0] if fields else None


def _process_start_time(pid: Any) -> str | None:
    """Read the kernel start tick that distinguishes reused process ids."""
    fields = _process_stat_fields(pid)
    return fields[19] if len(fields) > 19 else None

A NEW DEFECT IN THE GC SURFACE, distinct from the repository-scoping one this section landed, found while doing the session's mandatory cleanup. reckon crew gc DOES NOT COMPLETE on this repository. Killed at 100 seconds with no output; a first attempt was killed by the harness at its own ceiling and printed a truncated traceback from inside _inspect_workspace. The cause is scale rather than a crash: the repository carries 183 worktrees, and the two git calls gc makes per workspace cost 396 milliseconds each on this filesystem, so the serial inspection alone is about 72 seconds before any ledger lookup or reachability check. THE FEEDBACK LOOP IS THE FINDING. Cleanup that takes longer than an operator will wait does not get run; worktrees accumulate; the next run is slower. One hundred and eighty-three worktrees is not the starting condition this tool was written against, it is the RESULT of the tool being unusable, and the number grows monotonically with every session that gives up on it. This session's own cleanup was done by hand instead - twenty-three worktrees, each checked for the two conditions the rule requires, clean AND reachable from the integrated branch, then removed without forcing, none refused. That worked and it is not a substitute: a coordinator who does not know the two conditions, or who is tired at the end of a long session, will skip it, which is precisely how the backlog formed. What the surface needs is to report before it inspects everything - a count and a first page rather than a complete answer, so an operator learns the scale before deciding to wait - and to parallelise or cache the per-workspace reads. CONCEDING the refutation and REFUTING its mechanism, both measured. The finding is wrong: 957c042 is reachable from origin/main and was already reachable when I published the claim, so the ledger row is honest and this plan should carry no such defect. That much is settled.

The stated mechanism is not what happened, and it matters because it prescribes a fix that would not have prevented this. The claim was not a stale ref that wanted a fetch. This clone's reflog records the peer's landing as 4f5c404 refs/remotes/origin/main@{2026-09-03 10:49:05}: update by push — update by push, not fetch. We share one ref store: twenty-one worktrees hang off a single .git, so a peer's push updates the remote-tracking ref directly and there is nothing to fetch. Inserting git fetch ahead of the judgement would have changed the answer by nothing at all.

What actually happened is shelf life. The merge 862d8cf was created at 10:46:24 and the ref moved at 10:49:05; my finding was authored at 10:50:27. Since the check returned not reachable, it must have run before 10:49:05 — when that was the correct answer. The measurement was right and the claim was stale: it was published at least eighty-two seconds after it stopped being true, into a wave putting four pushes on main inside twenty-one minutes. I measured correctly and then let the answer age between the instrument and the prose.

So the measure changes shape. Reachability is not a fact, it is a reading with a shelf life, and during a live wave that shelf life is shorter than the time it takes to write a paragraph. Promotion must re-derive it at the instant it records the verdict rather than carrying an earlier reading forward, and must stamp the verdict with the time it was taken, because a reachability claim with no timestamp gives a reader no way to judge whether it has expired. Fetch-before-judging stays in the mechanism for the case it does address — a separate clone or a CI checkout, where the ref genuinely can lag — but it is hygiene here, not the remedy.

The agreed half is unchanged and I still want it: promotion verifies that a recorded commit is reachable from the integration branch or records explicitly that it is not. The peer would have been glad of it an hour earlier in the opposite direction, promoting five spend-limit deaths and needing to know which worktrees held commits, and that direction is the one where a false negative is cheap and a false positive loses work.

One note against myself, since it is the same failure as the count I corrected an hour ago wearing different clothes. There the instrument was aimed at prose instead of the event; here the instrument was aimed correctly and the reading was published after it expired. Both produce a confident wrong number, and both were caught by someone re-measuring rather than by me re-reading.

Two defects in the spend fence, reported by the imas-codex session and reproduced here before acceptance. The reproduction changed the operational conclusion while confirming both mechanisms, which is the reason to reproduce.

FIRST, A REJECTION-DERIVED HOLD NEVER EXPIRES. Two holds sit side by side in one file: a codex hold carrying resets_at: 2026-09-08T05:38:19Z, read from an account surface that publishes it, and hold-claude-opus-20260903100221 carrying resets_at: null because it was inferred from a worker's own 429. Dispatch therefore refuses that lane indefinitely at “utilisation 100.0% is at or above the 95.0% ceiling”. The datum is not absent, it is unparsed — the rejection text reads your session limit resets 3:40pm (Europe/Paris), one clause away from the field that would make the fence expire. Same shape as the unifiedWindows.five_hour.utilization figure the earlier hold could not read: a signal that exists and nothing consumes.

THE COST IS LARGER THAN A LANE THAT STAYS SHUT, AND THIS EXCHANGE IS THE EVIDENCE. The peer read the hold as stale and offered to have it closed; their user reported the account had reset. It had not. opened_at is written from checked_at (ledger.py:1070), and these stamps are genuine UTC — established by running crew preflight at 12:07 CEST and reading back checked_at: 2026-09-03T10:07:26Z, not by assuming. So the hold was opened 12:02:21 CEST, four minutes before it was read, from a denial whose stated reset is 15:40. Two accounts are in play: the on-the-hour one behind the claude lane did roll over at 12pm, and the 3:40pm one behind claude-opus did not. Closing that hold would have put nodes into a lane denied for another three and a half hours, where a hard 429 kills the turn with no diff and no manifest. So resets_at: null does not merely latch a fence — it makes a live fence and a stale one indistinguishable, and the reasonable reading of an unlabelled fence is the wrong one. Parsing the clause would have made the hold read resets_at: 2026-09-03T13:40:00Z, self-lift at 15:40, and settle the question without a stream corpus and a timezone experiment.

SECOND, PREFLIGHT AND DISPATCH DISAGREE ABOUT THE SAME LANE AT THE SAME INSTANT. Reproduced verbatim: preflight --role implement returns held: false, clear_backends: ['claude'], held_backends: [], enumerating one backend from a 2026-08-22 ledger record — while naming hold_history.path as the very file holding four open holds at version 1416, claude-opus among them. It reads that file for history and never folds its open holds into held_backends. Dispatch on the same lane a moment later refuses with a budget hold. The pre-flight an operator is told to run before opening a wave reports clear for a lane the dispatcher then refuses, and does not name the backend that is actually held. A third disagreement sits in the same payload: preflight reports utilisation_ceiling_pct: 100.0 while the refusal cites an effective ceiling of 95.0, so the two surfaces do not agree on the threshold either.

Worth recording what the peer did, because it is the behaviour the fence is for: they routed the node to the local lane rather than looking for an override, and it is running on deepseek-v4-flash. Fourth time today the local lane carried work a metered one could not, and the first time it was a fence rather than a real denial that sent it there — which is the case this section has to stop producing.

SUPERSEDING THIS SECTION'S OWN OVERAGE OBLIGATION, on the peer's correction, with the epochs verified here rather than taken. Earlier in this section we wrote that the fence owes a hold on an over-line overage warning with surpassedThreshold: 1, in the same place it holds on recorded utilisation. That is wrong, and it would have been an expensive kind of wrong: a fence that refuses correctly-serving lanes is indistinguishable from a spent account to everyone downstream, and it is the same latch failure as resets_at: null approached from the other side.

One serving stream carries both figures and they disagree. overage reads utilization 1.21, surpassedThreshold 1, isUsingOverage false; unifiedWindows.five_hour reads utilization 0.05. The lane was 54 turns in with zero rejections, so the window figure is the one describing reality. The two are not the same horizon: five_hour.resetsAt of 1788447600 is 2026-09-03 15:00 UTC, five hours after the 12pm rollover, while the overage record's 1790812800 is 2026-10-01 00:00 UTC. The peer read that second epoch as 2026-09-24; it is in fact the month boundary, which makes their point stronger than they put it — the overage counter is the account's calendar-month position and would have held every wave for the remaining four weeks of September.

So the figure to fence on is unifiedWindows.<period>.utilization against that window's own resetsAt. Recorded as a measure above; the superseded obligation stays in place as the record of how it was got wrong.

Owning the pre-flight item at the peer's request, since it belongs beside the other two faces of this blind spot rather than split for credit: enumerate the open holds from the file pre-flight already names into held_backends, and populate headroom from the newest window figure instead of leaving an August “unknown” standing. The window-versus-overage correction stays theirs. Worth noting the pattern across all four faces in this section — unasked, unparsed, unenumerated, and now misaimed — every one of them a signal that existed in a record nothing read correctly, which is this plan's whole subject arriving in the budget fence four separate ways.

TWO STATES FOR ONE CONDITION, found while checking a peer's report that the pane calls finished work abandoned. Their diagnosis does not survive measurement; the defect underneath it is real and is mine.

The peer observed abandoned firing 14 times with 13 recovering straight to promoted, and read 17 of 18 as having had a terminal manifest at that moment. They proposed a new unpromoted state keyed on process gone plus no terminal manifest. That predicate already exists and already wins: _watch_snapshot arbitrates manifest_status in {complete, blocked, failed} before the liveness check, so a dead run with a terminal manifest never reaches abandoned. Probed both directions on synthetic pointers, then measured the nine real live pointers: zero showing abandoned with a terminal manifest, two correctly at complete, one at blocked, and three at abandoned of which two have no manifest and one is in-progress. Every label correct.

The likely mechanism for their 14 is retrospective measurement, the failure this session has now produced three times: the manifests were read now rather than at classification time, and a worker whose process exits before its manifest lands makes abandoned correct at that instant and wrong shortly after. The discriminating test is manifest mtime against the transition timestamp, and the expected true sequence is dispatched → abandoned → complete → promoted with the third step short enough for the pane to elide. Left open pending their check; if a manifest predates its transition there is a real bug beneath this.

THE DEFECT THEIR REPORT DOES EXPOSE is a vocabulary duplicate. Two distinct states mean finished, waiting on the orchestrator: complete, which renders as “complete”, and completed_unpromoted, which renders as “unpromoted” through the DISPLAY map. Both sit in FLEET_UNPROMOTED_STATES and both feed the footer's unpromoted count, so the footer and the row can describe the same run with different words while the count stays right. That is the disagreement the peer saw, arrived at by a different route than they proposed — not a missing state but a redundant one, and the word shown for the common case is the one that does not tell an operator what to do next. Collapse the pair onto unpromoted.

Worth noting against this section's own standing obligation: the label was not derived from a missing signal here. Both halves of the predicate were in hand and the arbitration was correct. What was wrong was a second name for a state that already had one, which is the cheapest kind of display defect to introduce and the hardest to see from inside the code.

reckon-2d · 2026-09-03

ROOT CAUSE OF THE ABANDONED LABEL, and it retires both of my explanations for it. The manifests were terminal, they were at the path the classifier reads, and the parser returned without the status field.

The peer ran the mtime test I proposed and it came back against me: eight manifests were terminal on disk 4 to 63 seconds before the transition that labelled their run abandoned, and 63 seconds is past arguing as clock skew. I then guessed a second time, that they had measured a report rather than a manifest, because those run directories hold no manifest.md. The ledger settles that against me too — for n-audits-resolve-retired-spellings the recorded manifest_path is …/crew/reports/audits-resolve-retired-spellings.json. That file is the manifest. Their mtimes were measurements of exactly the file the classifier opens, both times.

The defect is the parse. On that file, parse_manifest returns status: None while json.loads returns status: 'complete'. The file is JSON; the reader expects the key: value text form. It does not refuse. It extracts the eight keys it happens to recognise — after_suite, artifacts, baseline_suite, blockers, changed_paths, commits, evidence_inputs, failure_attribution — and comes back indistinguishable from a well-formed manifest whose author omitted a status. So manifest_status is empty, the terminal arbitration has nothing to arbitrate, control reaches elif alive is False, and the run is labelled abandoned. The ordering argument I made in this section's defence was correct and irrelevant: the arbitration runs first, on an empty string.

48 runs carry a .json manifest_path — 37 in imas-codex, 11 in imas-ambix — plus one live pointer at the time of measurement. Two projects and two sessions, so this is a system defect rather than one session's habit, and every one of those nodes displays as abandoned from process exit until promotion. The dispatch accepted --manifest <path>.json without either supporting the format or rejecting it, which is where the mismatch entered; the silent partial parse is what made it invisible.

This is the cleanest instance of this plan's subject yet found. The other four faces were signals unasked, unparsed, unenumerated and misaimed. Here the record was read, from the correct path, at the correct time, by a reader that reported success having dropped the only field that mattered. A partial parse is worse than a refusal precisely because it is well-formed: nothing downstream can separate a format mismatch from a missing field.

ONE MORE, FROM THE PEER, AND IT IS THE REASON THIS TOOK ALL SESSION. The earlier ticker truncated the reason to “the process is gone without a…”, which reads as a generic liveness statement; the full string is “the process is gone without a complete manifest”, which names a predicate about a specific file and is therefore testable. They read the truncated form for hours. Truncation converted an instrument into a display, silently, and the whole investigation followed from restoring the sentence.

THE GUARD ALREADY EXISTED, WAS CORRECT, AND DID NOT RUN. This is the sharpest thing the day produced and the error is mine, in gate selection rather than in code.

tests/test_crew_monitor_output.py::test_every_emitted_state_lands_in_exactly_one_fleet_bucket has been in the tree since 09-01. It reads the emitted vocabulary out of _watch_snapshot by source scan, unions RECOVERY_CLASSES, and asserts emitted <= counted against the three fleet buckets — precisely the invariant that unreadable broke two days later.

Proven rather than inferred. Extracting the tree at 0627304, the commit that added the state, and running that one test: AssertionError: uncounted states: ['unreadable']. So the guard would have failed at the exact moment the gap opened.

It did not run because the gate I wrote for that node named test_crew_recovery, test_crew, test_crew_ticker, test_gate_evidence and test_manifest_parse_format, and the guard lives in none of them. I hand-listed the gate. The standing rule says to derive it from what changed — the tests covering the written paths plus any file that imports what changed — and test_crew_monitor_output.py imports recovery, so a derived gate would have included it and a hand-written one did not.

The cost was not the bug, which a peer's unrelated reconciliation closed within hours. The cost is that we then spent a node writing a second guard for an invariant that already had a correct one. The worker found the overlap itself and reported it rather than quietly duplicating, which is the only reason it is visible.

So the measure this section owes is not another assertion. A node's gate is derived from its write paths, never hand-listed — every test file that imports a changed module is in the gate, computed rather than remembered. Hand-listing is exactly the failure this plan keeps finding in other surfaces: a check that exists, is correct, and is never reached. I have been writing that finding about the code all day while producing it in my own dispatch.

SIX DEFECTS QUEUED BEHIND recovery.py AND runs.py, each measured on a live fleet today and recorded here so they survive a context boundary rather than living in a message channel. A node currently holds both files for the state-vocabulary repair; these follow it. (1) LIVENESS READS A ZOMBIE AS ALIVE. process_alive uses os.kill(pid, 0), which SUCCEEDS against a zombie because the process-table entry still exists, so a dead run awaiting reap is reported running and crew resume refuses it. Confirmed against a real defunct pid. This is the THIRD defect in that one call today: it returned False on PermissionError, reading a live process owned by another user as dead, and now True on a zombie, reading a corpse as alive. Both were confident wrong verdicts from a single syscall that cannot distinguish the cases. The remedy is to consult the process state and treat Z as dead. (2) A RESUME LEAVES ITS CHILD UNREAPED. The zombie above existed because a resume-ready sweep launched a child that finished and was never waited on. Better than tolerating zombies: the resume should waitpid its child or spawn it detached, so no corpse exists for any liveness check to trip over. (3) wait_terminal SPLITS A STRING ON COMMAS WITHOUT JSON-DECODING while its neighbour wait_probe does decode, so a manifest written with the natural JSON list produces terminal values that can never match and the run parks forever. (4) wait_started_at IS OPTIONAL WHEN ABSENT — mtime is the fallback — BUT REJECTED WHEN PRESENT AND UNPARSEABLE, so omitting the field is safe and writing it quoted is fatal, and a YAML-minded worker writes it quoted. (5) THE condition-overdue LABEL FIRES ON AGE ALONE even when the probe matched nothing, so it reads as 'the condition has been met for too long' and hides the real cause. A resumed run's pointer carries no trace of the attempt that failed, so the artifact a diagnostician most needs is the one the recovery destroys. Its prompt.txt is 10,291 bytes against a 480,000-token window, so the node contract was never the large term. This session diagnosed it confidently as a resumed long-lived transcript invisible to the context-fit estimator — the cause found here earlier in the day — and was wrong on every supporting fact.

Read asActually
argv carries --resume <id>, so the dispatch resumed a sessionthe pointer is attempt: 2, attempt_kind: "resume", started 10:46:50Z against the run's created_at of 10:39:10Z — the --resume is the recovery, and attempt 1's own system/init shows that session being created by the attempt that died
session_reuse: True confirms a session was reusedmeasured across every live pointer on this workstation: true on 51 of 51, and 45 of those carry no session_id at all — it reports that reuse is enabled, never that it occurred
the estimate was too lowthe estimate does not order the failures: the refused run computed 63,980 while two runs at 203,687 and 147,955 work normally on the same lane and model

session_reuse is a constant and should be treated as a defect in its own right. A field true in every case discriminates nothing, which is precisely why this plan retired the gate measure that sat at 1.00 on every lane. It is worse than a missing field, because a reader reaches for it and it answers.

What is established about the failure itself is narrow and stays that way: a brand-new session, a 10,291-byte prompt, a computed estimate of 63,980 against a 480,000 window, refused client-side in 300 ms. No root cause. The earlier resumed-transcript finding stands on its own evidence and has simply lost the cross-project confirmation that was making it feel solid.

The rule, which belongs in the classifier repair rather than in a note. Recovery and diagnosis are in direct tension and nothing in the surface says so: a coordinator following the documented remedy — resume rather than redispatch — overwrites the record of what it is remedying. So a run refused at admission needs a classification of its own carrying those four marks, and the failing attempt's record must survive the resume that follows it. At present the only durable evidence is three lines of stream.jsonl and a stderr.log the pointer no longer describes.

The generic abandoned bucket has a measured cross-fleet cost besides. Reading that death as a known local-lane defect, the reporting coordinator told a third fleet they had a second instance of a serve reliability problem; that fleet's own discriminator scores zero on both of its terms, so it was never that shape, and the report was retracted. Correction and refinement to the comment above, from the imas-codex fleet, and it breaks the repair this session had committed to. The finding recorded in c-the-wait-alarm-scored-zero-in-a-measured-wave is sound — both alarms were false and both workers were mid-turn — but the diagnosis attached to it was only half the mechanism, and the half that was missing is the one that invalidates the proposed fix.

The display ages the wrong artifact. wait-aged ages the manifest field, and the manifest is precisely the artifact a busy worker stops touching. Measured here on the same two runs, at one instant:

review-of-a-nested-key-stays-nested    manifest age 1838s   stream age 0s
an-audit-error-a-reader-cannot-clear   manifest age 1672s   stream age 3s

So the signal is structurally anti-correlated with what it detects: the longer a worker genuinely works, the more certainly it is reported stalled. The evidence that settles it is already in the run directory and is not consulted. The remedy is cheap — age on the stream's freshness, or render both so a reader sees 1838s since manifest, 0s since output and the contradiction resolves itself. This holds even for an entirely honest wait, which is what makes it the more general of the two defects.

And the probe is a constant, which is the layer that breaks the planned repair. The brief prepared here required a declared wait to carry a probe that runs and a terminal that can be reached. Reading the two blocks:

wait_probe: ["echo","pending"]          wait_terminal: exit:0
wait_probe: ["git","rev-parse","HEAD"]  wait_terminal: exit:0

Both probes run. Both terminals are reachable. Both are satisfied unconditionally. That falsifier would have passed them clean, and the repair would have shipped as a fix that fixes nothing. The discriminator is not well-formedness but whether the probe's result can ever differ: a wait must reference something outside the worker — a job id, a pid, a port, a path — never a command that cannot fail.

One of the two workers wrote wait_condition: orientation only — superseded by later writes in this turn. It knew its record was stale and had no way to say so except by rewriting a manifest it was too busy to rewrite. That sentence is the whole defect in the worker's own words.

Adjacent, from the same reporter and worth carrying wherever these states are documented: on that backend an orientation-time wait row is weak evidence in either direction, and three transient unreadable samples there self-corrected within about 40 seconds. Those were genuine mid-write reads, not defects — the difference between an instrument being wrong and an instrument catching a file mid-write, where only the first is a fault.

A run reported ! decide: the manifest reports a blocker over a manifest that says blockers: none. Measured here on a-run-record-says-whether-it-resumed, and it completes a family this plan has now seen three times in one day.

status: blocked
blockers: none
checkpoint: orientation done; defect confirmed by measurement …
            Next: rename the record's capability field and add the
            launch-carried observation, plus the focused test file.

The worker was not blocked. It ran out of turn mid-task, wrote an accurate checkpoint naming exactly what remained, and set a status word that did not match the blocker field beside it. The display took the word. The coordinator was then asked to decide something with no subject, and the cost was a read of the manifest to discover there was nothing to decide. Resume with advice returned it to working in forty seconds, with its session and every turn intact.

The family, stated once. Three distinct states today were inferred from a field that is not the authority for them:

StateRead fromThe authority it should read
wait-agedthe manifest's agethe stream's freshness — the manifest is what a busy worker stops touching
session_reusethe backend's capability flagwhether this run's own launch carried a prior session
blockedthe status wordwhether a blocker is recorded

Each is confident, wrong, and indistinguishable from correct at the point of reading — which is this plan's subject exactly. The blocked case is the cheapest to repair and the easiest to state as a rule: a status of blocked with no blocker recorded is a checkpoint, not a decision, and should classify as one rather than raising a demand.

Worth noting where the worker was right, since a day of defect-recording distorts the picture: it re-measured the population rather than trusting the brief's figure, and improved it — 51 of 51 pointers carrying session_reuse true with 47 holding no session id against the brief's 45, and exactly one carrying a resume flag in argv. The brief told it to re-measure because the population moves; it did, and the single positive case it found is the right thing to build the falsifier around.

Five separate defects were found in the manifest reader in a single day, all silent, and three of them reach commits — the field a promotion verifies a run by. Listing them together because the fifth was found by reading a worker's own manifest, and at that point the count stops being a series of incidents.

DefectEffectFound by
a quoted scalar kept its quotesthe whole manifest refused over one field's formattinga plan section
an off-vocabulary status wordthe whole manifest refused; run permanently unreadable, its claim blocking a stranger's promotion two days latera stuck run
a nested key hoisted to top levela commits entry indented under another parent became the run's declared commitsa follow-on drain
a block scalar swallowed every later fieldin a wholly indented manifest, commits returned emptyan independent review
a list of mappings flattened to stringscommits parsed as ['sha: 7f7541d3…'] — the line, key included, which can never resolve as a git refreading a worker's manifest

This is not five incidents. It is one format loose enough that workers improvise inside it, and one bespoke reader that absorbs each improvisation differently. Every one of the five was written by a worker doing something reasonable: quoting a scalar the way YAML allows, choosing a plausible synonym for a status, indenting a block, using a mapping list to carry a commit with its subject. None was malformed by any standard except this reader's.

The cost is concentrated rather than spread. commits is reachable by three of the five, and a promotion records what the reader returns — so a manifest written in any of those three shapes yields a ledger row whose commit reference is wrong, empty, or unresolvable, reported as a successful landing. This project's ledger already carries 9 unresolvable or unmerged commit references out of 879, and three of those resolve in sibling repositories, which is a different defect again.

The decision this raises is whether the sixth repair should be a repair at all. Each of the five was individually small and each was correctly scoped, but the sequence is evidence about the format rather than about any one patch. Two honest directions: adopt a strict parse with an explicit schema and refuse anything outside it, which makes workers' improvisation loud instead of silently reinterpreted; or keep the permissive reader and give it a conformance suite over the shapes workers actually emit, harvested from the manifests already on disk. The first costs worker retries, the second costs a corpus nobody has built.

What should not happen is a sixth patch landed on the assumption that the fifth was the last one. Four of these were found in a single day by looking, and nobody has yet looked systematically.

A sixth defect in the manifest reader, found four hours after the fifth, and it corrupts commits again — the fourth of the six to do so. Recording it because it arrived after the decision above was written, which is itself the argument.

A worker committed three changes and wrote them into its manifest. The reader returned five entries:

["c754cfe2 feat(crew): narrow or release a live run's write claim through a checked module",
 "bd79bf77 test(crew): a claimed path is released through the module and still refuses a live worker",
 "09a668dd test(crew): cover partial release",
 "an undeclared path",
 "a no-op narrowing and the promotion control"]

The third commit's subject is “cover partial release, an undeclared path, a no-op narrowing and the promotion control”. The reader split it on its own commas. Two of the five entries are prose fragments that can never resolve as git refs, and had that run been promoted as written, its ledger row would have carried them. That is a plausible origin for at least some of the nine unresolvable or unmerged commit references already sitting in this project's ledger, alongside the three that resolve only in sibling repositories.

Why this forces the decision rather than adding to it. The five defects listed above were found by looking; this one was found by reading one worker's manifest in passing, hours later, with nobody searching. Six defects in one reader in one day, four of them reaching the single field a promotion verifies a run by, and the sixth discovered incidentally — that is not a backlog being worked down, it is a sampling rate. Nobody has yet read the corpus of manifests on disk, and the last two defects were found without trying.

The worker was told to work around it by writing bare forty-character shas with no subject on the line, and told explicitly that this is a reader defect rather than a correction of what it wrote. That workaround is a coordinator carrying a parser's gap in a dispatch brief, which is precisely what this plan's sibling exists to stop.

unknown · undated

The six defects above are one defect. Measured directly rather than inferred: parse_manifest returns a string for every value, and list-valued fields are recovered afterwards by splitting that string on commas.

WrittenReturned
flat scalar'value' — correct
inline JSON object'{"a": 1, "b": 2}' — a string, never parsed
nested mapping'' — silently empty
list of mappings'a: 1, a: 2' — flattened, keys retained
list of scalars'one, two' — comma-joined

And the recovery, which is where the damage lands:

commits:
  - abc1234 fix(x): a change, with a comma
  - def5678 fix(y): plain

-> ['abc1234 fix(x): a change', 'with a comma', 'def5678 fix(y): plain']

So every one of the six is the same mechanism seen from a different field. A nested key leaks because there is no nesting. A block scalar swallows later fields because there is no block. A mapping list keeps its keys because there are no mappings. A commit subject splits because a list is a comma-joined string. A quoted scalar kept its quotes because the value was never a value. The reader is a flat string map wearing a structured interface, and every consumer reconstructs the structure it needs by string surgery, independently and differently.

Two consequences worth stating separately. First, the damage concentrates on commits because that field is list-valued, contains free text, and is the one a promotion verifies a run by — so it is simultaneously the most likely to contain a comma and the most costly to get wrong. Second, a nested mapping returning the empty string is worse than any of the others, because it is the only one that loses evidence silently and completely: a manifest carrying a full, well-formed tests block reads as having run no tests at all. That was measured on a node whose real result was 8 failed 310 passed at base against 8 failed 320 passed at head, zero added, and whose gate evidence the reader reported as absent.

This settles the decision recorded above. A seventh patch would repair one more field's string surgery. The choice is between giving the reader real structure — parse the document once, return mappings and lists as mappings and lists — or declaring the format flat and forbidding structured fields outright, so workers stop writing what cannot be read. Both are defensible; continuing to patch consumers is not, because the consumers are not where the defect is.

A resume that dies before writing anything leaves a zero-byte log, and the session resolver then reports the run unresumable while two surviving logs carry the answer. Measured today on a run with green tests in its worktree.

The sequence: a node was resumed moments before the local lane was taken down for a restart. The launch reached a dead backend, wrote nothing, and left resume-2.jsonl at 0 bytes. A later resume was refused:

no session id in any authority: no session id in the live pointer, the run's own
stream or the promoted ledger row; all three were consulted, so this is an
absence rather than a reading nobody has taken yet

Both older logs carried it:

stream.jsonl     4,197,269 bytes   session_id=476ca4aa-3108-418a-9008-5fd2205c43e6
resume-1.jsonl     279,574 bytes   session_id=476ca4aa-3108-418a-9008-5fd2205c43e6
resume-2.jsonl           0 bytes   (no parsable record)

The refusal is worse than a silent absence because it asserts its own thoroughness. That final clause exists to tell a reader not to go looking — it explicitly distinguishes a real absence from an unmade reading, and it is wrong in exactly the way it promises not to be. A coordinator who trusts it discards a recoverable run; this one only looked because the sentence was too confident to be worth believing after a day of instruments that answer adjacent questions.

The remedy is narrow. The resolver consults the newest log per source; it should consult the newest log that parses, or fall back through the run's logs in order. A failed launch is exactly when a resume is most needed and exactly when the newest artifact is emptiest, so the two conditions coincide by construction rather than by coincidence.

Recovered by restoring session_id to the pointer from the value both surviving logs carry, which is what the resolver would have done had it looked past the empty file. Verified first that an earlier hand edit to that pointer had not caused it: diffed against the backup taken before that edit, and session_id was already null there, with node the only field changed. Given the coordinator had edited shared state minutes earlier to work around a missing command, ruling that out was the first obligation rather than the last.

Related to the followup above on the pointer's session field lagging its authority: that one is a field trailing a resolver that works, this one is the resolver itself aiming at the wrong artifact. Same family, opposite halves.

Held unmerged: the arrival extraction drops the row it was built to catch. Run r-20260917T165959552736 delivered three commits and an independent review scored it 72/100 — goal_fidelity 12, durability 12, evidence 13 — with seven findings. It is not merged and not promoted, and its live pointer is deliberately preserved so the session can be resumed rather than redispatched.

The headline finding, verified here rather than taken from the review. In _rendered_row the transition branch reads if len(left) < 2 or len(tokens) < 2: return None. A rendered transition row whose only token left of the arrow is the node name — which is precisely what a node's first appearance looks like, having no source state — gives tokens of length one and returns None. The arrival is dropped. The reviewer's sample is direct and reproducible: in the imas-ambix stream, line 1 reads 16:29:36 clive-reuse-map -> dispatched and is discarded, and extract_watch_arrivals returns line 4 instead. The function's own docstring promises the rendered form is marked as carrying no establishable stamp rather than dropped silently, so the code contradicts its own stated contract.

Two further findings that would have survived a merge indefinitely. The only rendered baseline fixture in the seven new tests is a bullet line, a shape that occurs zero times across all six live streams — so the suite ranges over a form the corpus never produces and could not have caught the defect above. And the evidence record states that 2,317 of 2,931 nodes present no transition row, where the corpus gives 14 of 2,951: a figure wrong by two orders of magnitude, published as a landed measurement.

The remaining findings concern a population count that tallies nodes carrying a JSON row rather than the nodes the function sees, and a burst test whose failure direction is itself a dropped arrival.

Disposition. Scope discipline was clean at 20/20 and the worktree is clean, so nothing here is a boundary problem — the node did what it was asked, and what it was asked does not hold. Resume with advice naming the one-token case as the falsifier, rather than redispatching, because the session holds the context and a redispatch discards it.

The resume advice, recorded here so it is not reconstructed from memory: a rendered transition row whose only token left of the arrow is the node name is an arrival and must be returned, not dropped. Write that falsifier first and confirm it fails at the current head. Then replace the bullet-line fixture with shapes drawn from the live streams, naming the source stream for each. Then re-derive the 2,317-of-2,931 figure and state the derivation beside it. Do not promote until the one-token case passes; promotion deletes the pointer and takes the resumable session with it.

A regression this plan's own work introduced, and the node repairing it. The declared-schema reader that landed on 2026-09-17 fixed four measured defects and broke twenty-seven manifests the line-scanning reader had accepted. The repair node is the-declared-schema-reads-what-the-old-reader-read, and this comment exists so that node's reason survives the session that cut it.

How it was measured. The previous reader was extracted from eb74752d~1 and both readers were run over every manifest under the crew configuration home — 3,694 files. Two thousand eight hundred and ninety-five parse under both. Thirty that the old reader refused now parse, which is the change doing its job. Twenty-seven that the old reader accepted are now refused, in four shapes: thirteen on test_logs, eleven on artifacts, one on follow_ons and one on commits, each reporting that the field carries a mapping where the schema expects a list. A twenty-eighth is not a refusal but a crash, TypeError: cannot use 'dict' as a dict key.

The corpus is durable rather than in a session scratchpad. The twenty-seven paths, one per line, are at ~/.config/reckon/crew/reports/reader-regression-corpus.txt. Any later reader can re-derive the comparison from it without rebuilding the extraction.

Blast radius, and why this was not urgent. Zero live runs were affected when measured: all twenty-seven are historical manifests, so no follower was misreading a working fleet because of it. That is the reason the repair was queued behind other work rather than jumped ahead of it, and it is worth recording because the same defect with live runs in the set would have been a different decision.

The negative half the repair must keep. The four defects the schema was introduced to fix stay fixed: a commits list whose third subject contains a comma reads as three entries and not four, and a tests field written as a nested mapping reads as that mapping rather than the empty string. A repair that restores the twenty-seven by returning the reader to line scanning is a failure, not a pass.
