Four defects recorded on this plan today are one defect: a state word that was true when written, read as though it were true now, with nothing on the row carrying the age of the claim. The framing is the peer coordinator's; the instances were found separately, by two sessions, on four surfaces, none of us looking for a pattern.

WordReads asWhat it wasMeasured
promotedwork bankeda pointer departed — promotion, discard or rollback alikerecovery.py:2838; ledger holds 0 rows for the discarded run against 1,072
abandonedthe worker is goneit compacted; resumable throughout, back working 90s later25,594-char compaction document, attempt: 2 on resume
workingin progressprocess gone 22 minutes earlier, 353 insertions uncommittedthis session's own §2 node, caught by running the pattern as a query
blockedneeds a decisionstream 0 seconds old and writingtwo implement nodes live, both also reading status: in-progress

Every one is individually repairable and repairing them individually is the wrong response. Each has an obvious local fix — resolve promoted against a ledger row, read compaction before declaring abandonment, key liveness on stream freshness, reconcile phase with the manifest. Four fixes, four tests, and the fifth instance arrives next week in a state word nobody has enumerated, because the thing they share is not in any of them.

What they share is that a state is stored without its observation time. A classification is a measurement, and a measurement without a stamp cannot be compared against anything — not against the process table, not against the stream, not against a later reading of itself. The surface then has no way to express this was true at 16:31 and I have not looked since, so every reader supplies now for free, and is wrong in proportion to how long the row has sat.

The evidence that it is one defect rather than four is how they were found. No instance was found by looking for it. The discard came from a peer checking a counter it did not trust; the compaction from a diagnosis of mine that the run refuted by resuming; the dead-but-running from running the peer's own synthesis as a query against a live fleet; the blocked-but-writing from a glance at an unrelated field. Four surfaces, two coordinators, one afternoon, no search. A defect that dense is a property of the model rather than a run of bad luck in four modules.

The falsifier for treating it as one, and it is cheap. Give a stored state its observation time and require every reader to compare that stamp against the fact it is about — the process table, the newest stream mtime, the ledger. If the four instances then reduce to one rule and no new local checks are needed, the unification is real. If any of them still needs its own repair afterwards, it was four defects and this comment is wrong.

It is recorded here rather than under any of the four sections because it belongs to none of them, and because a plan titled for a display that cannot lie should carry the reason its display keeps lying in one place.

A second case for §25, from nova's S21 coordinator, forwarded by S25 on 2026-10-02. Three promoted-failed nova lineage worktrees hold unmerged commits that a live run builds on. gc --apply correctly refuses to remove them. drain --leave takes only run ids, and the obligations hook has no disposition for a deliberately retained tree, so the stop hook blocks every turn. The code is reckon/crew/obligations.py, around lines 411 to 457.

Suggested remedy: a retained tree reads as lineage-held, not as an obligation, when its HEAD is an ancestor of a live run's base or tip. Failing that, drain --leave accepts <worktree>=lineage-held, expiring when that run turns terminal. §25's done-when gains one case: a retained tree whose HEAD is an ancestor of a live run's base reads lineage-held, and it returns as an obligation once that run is terminal.

Coordinator ruling for node an-overrun-names-its-cause (r-20261003T130845405108), recorded because it reads this section's second measure narrowly and the lead may want it the other way.

The worker found one budget-driven signal path: _apply_budget_watchdog in reckon/crew/recovery.py, added at d5d3c3513 on 2026-08-17. That predates this section's directive (2026-09-09). The watchdog is gated on fences.enforce_budget_watchdog, which reckon/schema/flight-defaults.yaml sets to false. Four test files and the flight schema assert it. Removing it would delete an operator's opt-in ceiling against a runaway session, and the directive itself says the budget "exists to stop a runaway session, not to end a working one".

Ruling: the budget is a soft limit and nothing signals a worker on it. The watchdog is a separate, config-gated ceiling at budget times grace, off by default, and it stays. The call-graph test enumerates every signalling call reachable from budget or overrun computation and permits exactly that gated path. It asserts the shipped default is false, and that with the flag false the path signals nothing. Any other budget-driven signal fails it. If the directive is meant to forbid the opt-in ceiling too, the follow-on is to remove the watchdog, its four asserting test files and its schema key together, with a migration note for any config that sets it. None on this host does.
